courses.title: Lighting Technology
courses.description: This course combines lectures and lab demonstrations on the setup and use of lighting equipment, technology, and effects used in live events. Students learn of the available technology and its proper use and handling. Topics include power distribution, understanding DMX, plots, LED fixtures, moving lights, board programming, fog and haze units, and wired and wireless practicals. Open to non-TD&P and non-Drama students with prior permission of the instructor. Enrollments is limited to twenty.

courses.title: Theater Planning and Construction
courses.description: This course is an introduction to the planning, design, documentation, and construction of theaters, concert halls, and similar spaces. Emphasis is placed on the role of the theater consultant in functional planning and architectural design. The goal is to introduce the student to the field and provide a basic understanding of the processes and vocabulary of theater planning. Open to non-TD&P and non-Drama students with prior permission of the instructor. Matt Welander

courses.title: Projection Engineering
courses.description: This course provides students with the skills and vocabulary necessary to perform as projection engineers. Students are introduced to the paperwork to design, the equipment to implement, and the software to operate a successful video projection system while interfacing with a projection designer.
courses.requirements: Open to non-TD&P and non-Drama students with permission of the instructor.

courses.title: Revit for Theater Consultants
courses.description: DRAM 429a, Revit for Theater Consultants This fall course explores the basics of Autodesk Revit, Autodesk Construction Cloud, Bluebeam construction software, and their use in the planning and construction of performing arts buildings. Topics include architectural modeling and detailing, generating project deliverables, document management and model coordination, and family content creation. Open to non-TD&P and non-Drama students with prior permission of the instructor. DRAM 429b, Theater Engineering: Overhead Rigging and Stage Machinery This spring course introduces the basic concepts necessary to design overhead rigging and stage machinery systems for performing arts buildings. Topics include the role of the theater consultant in the architectural design process; programming, designing, and budgeting stage equipment; relevant standards and code requirements; and collaborating with other design disciplines to successfully integrate stage equipment and supporting infrastructure into the final building design. Open to non-TD&P students with prior permission of the instructor. Matt Welander

courses.title: Human Resources: Supporting People and Building Culture
courses.description: The postpandemic workplace has changed dramatically, introducing terms like "remote work," "hybrid," "the great resignation," "work-life balance," "AI," "digital connectivity," and "psychological safety." Sociopolitical, global, and economic forces have caused significant disruption and fatigue. In this new landscape, empathetic and resilient leaders are essential to fostering a supportive and inclusive workplace culture. This class explores current and evolving human resources practices in the American theater, a unique workplace comprising union and non-union members, full-time and seasonal staff, as well as artists and artisans engaged for short periods. The course examines employee engagement, recruitment, hiring, inclusion and belonging, compensation, benefits, legal issues, performance management, and wellness—all aimed at creating a thriving, healthy, and inspiring workplace. Open to non-Theater Management and non-Drama students with prior permission of the instructor. Florie Seery

courses.title: Principles of Marketing and Audience Development
courses.description: This survey course explores the fundamentals of nonprofit theater marketing, communications, and audience development. Topics range from high-level strategic components such as branding, positioning, audience research, and budgeting (revenue and expense); to campaign tactics including digital channels, direct marketing, traditional advertising, partnerships, and publicity; to data-driven practices such as segmentation, campaign response data/return on investment, and other key performance indicators. Students develop a single-ticket marketing plan.
courses.requirements: Open to non-Theater Management and non-Drama students with prior permission of the instructor.

courses.title: Producing for the Commercial Theater
courses.description: This course focuses on the fundamentals of commercial producing on Broadway. Among the topics to be covered: why produce commercially; who produces; Broadway and Off-Broadway; the relationships between commercial producers and nonprofits; and ethical issues in a commercial setting. Practical matters covered include optioning and developing work, raising money, creating budgets, and utilizing marketing/press/advertising to attract an audience.
courses.requirements: Open to non-Theater Management and non-Drama students with prior permission of the instructor.

courses.title: Readings in Modern Latin American History
courses.description: A readings course for doctoral students. It is geared especially for students in preparation for their exams or who are writing their prospectuses. Readings are selected according to the students’ interests, geared to help them move forward in the program.

courses.title: Investing Excellence
courses.description: This course taught by Jim Millar (formerly Princeton endowment) and Dean Takahashi (former Yale endowment), provides direct access to accomplished investors. Through case studies and simulated investment committee meetings, students will evaluate investment process and manager selection. This course is limited in capacity and requires a short pre-assignment. For more information about the assignment, MMS asset management students may contact: assetmanagement@yale.edu. The course is only open to SOM students in the Asset Management Master of Management Science program.

courses.title: College in Prison
courses.description: The history, present, and future of higher education in prison seen through the perspective of practitioners, students, alumni, faculty, theorists, and higher ed policymakers. Topics include: prison education and abolition; liberal arts in prison; the history of higher education in the U.S.; the 1994 Pell grant ban for incarcerated students and the restoration of Pell access; citizenship and education; town-gown relationships, reparations, and higher education; the idea of criminality and the idea of studenthood; and the history of the Yale student body.
courses.classnotes: Priority is given to Education Studies Certificate students and then by graduation year. Please indicate your interest in the course as well as major, EDST program participation, and whether you've taken EDST 1110.
courses.requirements: EDST 1110 recommended.

courses.title: Directed Studies: Literature
courses.description: An examination of major literary works with an aim of understanding how a tradition develops. In the fall term, works and authors include Homer, Aeschylus, Sophocles, Virgil, the Bible, and Dante. In the spring term, authors vary somewhat from year to year and include Petrarch, Cervantes, Shakespeare, Milton, Wordsworth, Goethe, Tolstoy, Proust, and Eliot.
courses.requirements: You must be an admitted student of the Directed Studies program in order to register for this course

courses.title: Advanced Graduate Seminar
courses.description: The course allows students to hone their presentation skills through yearly presentation of their dissertation work. Two students each give thirty-minute presentations in each class session. Students are required to present every year beginning in their third year in the MCDB program. Each MCDB graduate student is expected to attend at least 80 percent of the class sessions. Two faculty members co-direct the course, attend the seminars, and provide feedback to the students.

courses.title: Principles of Advanced Oncology Practice
courses.description: This course introduces students to the principles of advanced oncology nursing practice. It focuses on (1) the problem of cancer—the epidemiology, biology, genetics, and immunology of cancer; (2) advanced practice nursing across the cancer care continuum (prevention, detection, diagnosis, treatment, chronic illness, and end of life), emphasizing nursing strategies for promoting patient- and family-centered care; and (3) the treatment of cancer, exploring the mechanisms of action, efficacy, and short- and long-term side effects of experimental and common traditional anticancer treatment modalities, as well as complementary, palliative, and supportive care. Required of all students in the oncology concentration in the first year of specialization.
courses.requirements: Prerequisite: approval from primary specialty adviser and oncology coordinator.

courses.title: Gender and Sexuality Health Justice (GSHJ) Clinical
courses.description: This clinical conference course builds upon the experiences gained in specialty clinical courses. This clinical provides students further opportunity to develop advanced nursing skills with LGBTQI+ patients, including specialized clinical judgment and evidence-based patient management strategies learned from didactic learning in both their specialty programs and within the GSHJ classroom.

courses.title: Foundations of Entheogen-Assisted Care in Nursing
courses.description: This course provides registered nurses with a comprehensive introduction to the ever-evolving field of entheogen-assisted care. In this course, students explore key topics including various entheogenic compounds, their pharmacological properties, and therapeutic applications. Students engage with the historical and cultural contexts surrounding entheogenic use, including Indigenous practices and modern therapeutic settings. Legislative frameworks and pathways to access entheogenic therapies are examined, enabling students to understand both the opportunities and challenges within this respective field. The course is structured into weekly modules that cover various aspects of entheogens, their history, legal frameworks, ethical issues, and societal impacts. Through various teaching modalities, students develop a foundational knowledge base that prepares them for advanced therapeutic practices in the following semester.
courses.requirements: Only students in the final year of their M.S.N. are eligible for this course.

courses.title: Political Determinants of Health 1: Core Concepts for Population Health
courses.description: This course enables students to identify policy and political levers as interventions to address population health challenges. Students examine the political foundations of the health ecosystem and explore how civic engagement, advocacy, governance, law and policy, commercial interests, health reform, and equity movements shape population health outcomes. Various contemporary issues serve as focal points for discussion.
courses.requirements: Prerequisite: completion of first-year M.S.N.

courses.title: Clinical Practice II for Global Health Track
courses.description: This clinical application course for students in the global health track provides opportunities to develop advanced nursing skills with a range of global populations within the students’ areas of specialization. While in clinical settings, students develop skills in assessment and management of acute and chronic conditions using evidence-based patient management strategies in accordance with the cultural beliefs and practices of populations of immigrants, refugees, American Indians, and Alaskan native and rural residents. These experiences may take place in YSN-approved U.S. or international settings. Additional experiences with local resettlement organizations such as Integrated Refugee and Immigrant Services (IRIS) and Connecticut Institute for Refugees and Immigrants (CIRI) are also available. These experiences may include developing and presenting education programs to groups of refugees, immigrants, or asylum seekers; creating training materials for the resettlement agencies; or serving as a cultural companion or health navigator for newly arrived families. Required of all students pursuing the global health track during the fall term of their second specialty year. Thirty hours of face-to-face interactions either in a health care setting or in an alternative setting, and one hour per week of clinical conference. Taken after NURS 6230.

courses.title: Abortion Care Elective
courses.description: This course teaches foundational and advanced concepts of abortion care for nurse practitioners and midwives including the provision of medication abortion, aspiration abortion, and pre- and post-abortion care. Students engage with leaders in the field to understand essential issues related to direct care provision, scope of practice and other legal issues, training, reproductive justice, and advocacy. This course meets once for a eight-hour in-person education session and includes seven hours of asynchronous learning for a total of fifteen hours (1 credit). This is an elective course with limited spaces, open to all M.S.N. students. In fall, priority will be given to second-year CNM and WHNP students.

courses.title: Advanced Health Assessment
courses.description: This course is designed to provide the advanced practice and midwifery student with the fundamental knowledge and skills needed to conduct a comprehensive, focused health history and physical examination and includes core content regarding assessment of all human systems, advanced assessment techniques, concepts, and approaches. Emphasis is on the assessment of physical, psychosocial, spiritual, and cultural dimensions of health, as well as factors that influence behavioral responses to health and illness. Normal/abnormal variations in physical exam findings and differential diagnoses are presented. Content includes assessment of individuals of diverse and special populations, including transgender, LGBTQIA, geriatric, pediatric and individuals with disabilities. This course is required for all students in the first semester of M.S.N. program enrolled in the Adult/Gero Primary and Acute Care Specialties, Family Nurse Practitioner, Nurse Midwifery, Women’s Health and Psychiatric Mental Health Specialties.

courses.title: Psychiatric-Mental Health Clinical Practice III
courses.description: This is the third practicum in a series of four that aim to develop the clinical and leadership skills required for advanced psychiatric mental health nursing practice. Building on first year clinical skills, emphasis is placed on advancing clinical reasoning and decision making, beginning use of pharmacologic interventions and safe prescribing practices, performing and documenting comprehensive mental health assessments, guiding care coordination, and counseling patients, groups, and families on health promotion and disease prevention. Students continue to build systems-level thinking by analyzing population data against benchmarks, managing team interactions, and evaluating quality and safety in the practice environment. Students analyze the impact of structural and cultural factors on individual- and population-level care delivery and develop lifelong learning strategies. Students are assigned to psychiatric clinical placements to align with competency development, previous clinical experiences, and interests. Students use the clinical case conference format to integrate and apply clinical skills. Clinical case conference meets weekly; clinical practicum hours are 225 for this course.
courses.requirements: Prerequisite: Psychiatric-Mental Health Clinical Practice II.

courses.title: Psychotherapeutic Interventions II: Application and Special Populations
courses.description: This is the second course in a series of three courses that examine the practice and application of psychotherapy across the lifespan. Individual, group and family modalities are covered. Developmental and trauma-informed principles are applied in a therapeutic context. Specific interventions include relational, cognitive, and behavioral approaches. Modalities are discussed with application to children and adults, intergenerational processes, and group and family dynamics. Students are actively engaged in psychotherapeutic treatment planning, intervention, and evaluation. The course comprises 1.5 didactic hours (22.5 hours) and 0.5 (22.5 hours) lab hours. 2 credits.
courses.classnotes: Course meets in room 01105
courses.requirements: Prerequisite: successful completion of NURS 7615.

courses.title: Psychiatric-Mental Health Clinical Practice V
courses.description: This is the fifth course in a series of five courses that aim to develop the clinical and leadership skills required for advanced psychiatric mental health nursing practice. Emphasis will be placed on incorporating emerging evidence and innovation into clinical decision making, ordering and documenting diagnostic and screening tests, evaluating care outcomes, and adjusting the plan of care with the interprofessional team. Students are expected to foster community partnerships, participate in system level change initiatives, determine population priorities for care, and design policy to impact health equity. Students will expand their leadership skills by engaging in professional organization and professional service opportunities. In their clinical setting, students will collaboratively provide care for individuals, groups and families for complex presentations (>2 diagnoses) involving multiple systems engagement. Students are assigned to psychiatric clinical placements on the basis of competency development, previous clinical experiences, and interests. Students will use the clinical case conference format to integrate and apply clinical skills. Clinical case conference meets 1 hours per week with PMHNP faculty. Clinical practicum is a requisite 210 clinical hours for this course.
courses.requirements: Successful completion of N7785O, N7786O, and N7795O, and N7796O.

The student provides health care for children over the course of the year at selected pediatric primary care sites in the community. Required of all pediatric nurse practitioner primary care students in the final year. Fifteen hours of clinical conference and 168 hours of clinical practice.
courses.classnotes: Course meets in room 01105.

courses.title: Primary Care I: Introduction to FNP Practice
courses.description: This course introduces first-year family nurse practitioner (FNP) students to the basics surrounding advanced nursing clinical practice. It prepares students for advanced clinical practice by bridging the gap between RN and APRN roles and skill set. Students begin developing the critical thinking, clinical reasoning, and relational skills needed for advanced nursing care in a supportive learning environment. This course builds on concepts from the Advanced Health Assessment course, focusing on key elements of FNP practice such as history taking, chart review, clinical reasoning, skill refinement, and professional growth essential for first-year nurse practitioner students. Students meet weekly for a ninety-minute clinical seminar that is held concurrently with or without clinical practice. This course is required of all FNP students in the first semester of the first year of specialization.
courses.requirements: Prerequisites: RN license and FNP program admission.

courses.title: Beethoven Sonatas for Strings and Piano: Performance and Analysis
courses.description:
4 credits, NP. Group A. Instructor permission required; by audition only. Auditions will occur on Monday 8/31 through Sunday 9/6, by individual arrangement with the instructor. Interested students should contact Professor Friedmann at michael.friedmann@yale.edu.

The class addresses performance/analysis in 4-5 sonatas for violin or cello and piano by Beethoven. The experiences and musical affinities of class membership will be demonstrated by audition, and will help to determine the exact choice of repertoire. The School’s Regier fortepiano, tuned at A=430, will be played in rehearsals, classes and the final concert. Rudolf Kolisch’s article "Tempo and Character in Beethoven’s Music" provides a point of departure for discussion. At the same time, form, rhetoric, phrase structure, hypermeter, "topic" and harmonic design will all be explored insofar as these factors affect performance. Other Beethoven scores will be studied to the extent that they shed light on the works’ character. Light readings from books such as Charles Rosen’s Classical Style and Sonata Forms as well as WilIiam Caplin’s Classical Form will also be required.

The course culminates in a concert of the repertoire being studied. There will be two in-class quizzes which give students opportunity to exhibit command of the issues explored in the class and detailed knowledge of all the works being rehearsed. Frequent but brief written assignments will prepare students for detailed discussion of the music. Prompt submission of written work is essential.

courses.title: Legacies of Paul Verlaine: Music, Poetry, and Arts of the Belle Époque (1871-1914)
courses.description:
4 credits, NP. Group B. This interdisciplinary seminar begins with the poetry of Paul Verlaine and follows the remarkable network of artists, musicians, writers, painters, photographers, patrons, and performers connected to his life and legacy. Through Verlaine's relationships to figures including Claude Debussy, Gabriel Fauré, Reynaldo Hahn, Pauline Viardot, Félix Nadar, Édouard Manet, Claude Monet, Auguste Rodin, and many others, students explore the rich cultural landscape of nineteenth-century Paris and the burgeoning artistic modernism of the Belle Époque.

Approaching music, poetry, painting, photography, and history as conversations within a shared creative world, students will listen to (and at times perform) music, read poetry (translation provided), examine paintings, photographs, sculpture, manuscripts, and first editions, and engage directly with Yale's extraordinary collections through visits to the Yale University Art Gallery, the Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library, and the Irving S. Gilmore Music Library. Throughout the semester, students will consider how ideas circulated among artists through friendship, collaboration, salons, correspondence, publication, and performance. The course culminates in original interdisciplinary projects that trace each student's own artistic constellation from Verlaine into another creative world through research, performance, creative practice, digital humanities, or public scholarship.

courses.title: Muslims in the United States
courses.description: Since 9/11, cases of what has been termed "home-grown terrorism" have cemented the fear that "bad" Islam is not just something that exists far away, in distant lands. As a result, there has been an urgent interest to understand who American Muslims are by officials, experts, journalists, and the public. Although Muslims have been part of America’s story from its founding, Muslims have alternated from an invisible minority to the source of national moral panics, capturing national attention during political crises, as a cultural threat or even a potential fifth column. Today the stakes are high to understand what kinds of meanings and attachments connect Muslims in America to the Muslim world and to the US as a nation. Over the course of the semester, students grapple with how to define and apply the slippery concept of diaspora to different dispersed Muslim populations in the US, including racial and ethnic diasporas, trading diasporas, political diasporas, and others. By focusing on a range of communities-in-motion and a diverse set of cultural texts, students explore the ways mobility, loss, and communal identity are conceptualized by immigrants, expatriates, refugees, guest-workers, religious seekers, and exiles. To this end, we read histories, ethnographies, essays, policy papers, novels, poetry, memoirs; we watch documentary and fictional films; we listen to music, speeches, spoken word performances, and prayers. Our aim is to deepen our understanding of the multiple meanings and conceptual limits of homeland and diaspora for Muslims in America, particularly in the Age of Terror.

courses.title: Readings in Critical Muslim Studies
courses.description: This course surveys key texts from a broad range of fields, including transnational American studies, religious studies, history, and anthropology, to explore methodological and theoretical questions that include: What is the "critical" in critical Muslim studies? What and who is "the Muslim" in these scholarly formations: a religious subject, a racial category, a location of subjection and surveillance, or all of these? What theoretical frameworks have emerged in the past twenty years to analyze the Muslim experience, and what is the impact of these intellectual projects on the academy and Muslim populations themselves? What different methodologies are used and what kinds of knowledge do they yield? How does critical Muslim studies as an emergent field complicate notions of an "American Islam" and "American Islamophobia," terms that are and have been practiced, debated, encoded, and altered both by transnational populations within the United States and by U.S. imperial policies, investments, and interests in Islam. The aim is to combine the resources and insights of various disciplines while identifying theoretical and methodological pitfalls and possibilities for future research. We focus on the relationship of our readings to other interdisciplinary formations that transcend disciplines, such as critical security studies and the anthropology of the secular, and the debates and trends therein.
courses.requirements: Permission of the instructor required.

courses.title: Analysis of Biological Systems
courses.description: Biology is undergoing a rapid evolution from descriptive and largely qualitative science to data-rich and quantitative, mature discipline. However, given the complexity of biological processes and the still early stage of its development, it lacks a solid theoretical basis. What is becoming clear is that it is a science of systems, with new and frequently unexpected properties emerging from interaction of multiple components on different temporal and spatial scales. New physical, chemical, and mathematical principles are developed to understand these processes. This course is focused on learning the key concepts that have emerged over the last two decades that shape this new science and on the experiential, theoretical, and computational tools used in this research. These concepts will likely be shaping the twenty-first-century biology-driven advances in physics, chemistry, and biology, in understanding and engineering life and a new technologies that will emerge. The course is primarily aimed at graduate students with college-level background in math, physics, and chemistry. The biological concepts are introduced during the classes.
courses.requirements: Prerequisite: Basic knowledge of probability, linear algebra, and calculus is strongly preferred. Please consult with the instructor if in doubt.

courses.title: Advanced Microeconomic Theory III
courses.description: The course focuses on key concepts of microeconomic theory. Topics may include information design, theories of learning, decision theory, behavioral economics, and the economics of data.

courses.title: Senior Research Project and Colloquium
courses.description: Independent research under the supervision of members of the faculty, resulting in a senior essay. Students meet with peers and faculty members regularly throughout the fall term to discuss the progress of their research. Projects should offer substantial opportunity for interdisciplinary work on environmental problems. Seniors in the BS track typically write a two semester senior essay by enrolling in EVST 4960 and EVST 4960. For the B.A. degree, students most often complete one term of EVST 4960, in either the fall or spring semester of their senior year. Students writing the one-term essay in the BA track must also complete an additional advanced seminar in the environment. Two-term senior research projects in the BA track require the permission of the DUS. Single semester essays are permissible also for students completing a double major that involves writing a senior essay in another department or program with permission of the DUS and subject to Yale College academic regulations governing completion of two majors.
courses.classnotes: Section 04 is intended for EVST seniors who plan to complete their senior essays in Spring semester. This category includes students in the BS track, which requires a two-term senior essay, and those students in the BA track who have been approved by the EVST DUS to pursue a two-term project. For students in the BA track, enrollment in this section requires prior confirmation that the student has secured the commitment of a Yale faculty member to act as their senior essay advisor and the advisor's and the EVST DUS's approval of their proposed topic and plan of research. More information on the advising relationship and the senior essay process can be found in the EVST Senior Essay Handbook.

courses.title: Northwest Semitic Inscriptions: Official Aramaic
courses.description: Official Aramaic is the lingua franca of the Persian Empire during the sixth and fourth centuries BCE. This course is designed to familiarize students with texts from Achaemenid Egypt (the abundant papyri of Elephantine and Hermopolis), Bactria, Anatolia, and Mesopotamia. The Aramaic grammar is illustrated through the texts.
courses.requirements: Prerequisite: RLST 835, or some knowledge of Aramaic or a related Semitic language.

courses.title: Sustainable AI
courses.description: AI is increasingly embedded in all aspects of society. There are both utopian and dystopian scenarios, and everything in between. This course considers different scenarios: the perspective of business and the environment with a global perspective. The course covers the pros and cons of AI, from sustainability, societal and business perspectives and covers some of the leading actors in this space. It includes practical, real world examples from companies, governments and NGOs, with a focus on how AI is being used, for the greater good and also at times with unintended consequences. There are three main blocks: AI and the Environment, Risks and Governance, and Business and Society. The course includes external guest speakers who are experts in the field of business, sustainable AI, and other relevant subject matter experts. There is a mandatory field trip as well as group exercises. The course assumes students have a basic understanding of AI.

courses.title: Quantitative Foundations of General Chemistry Lab
courses.description: This laboratory affords students at the beginning of their science studies to have meaningful and foundational engagement with experimental chemistry. The lab equips students for further science laboratory classes and laboratory research in the sciences. The course is structured to take students with little or no prior exposure to practical work in the sciences through a series of experiments in which they use scientific apparatus and practice techniques that are core to experimental work in chemistry and other physical sciences. This includes experiments involving calorimetry, electrochemistry, volumetric analysis, computational chemistry, spectroscopy, and synthesis. Students finish with a strong grounding in laboratory safety and experimental design, as well as in the collection and recording of measured and observational data, in addition to exposure to the apparatus and software platforms common to many physical science laboratories. This lab qualifies students for the organic chemistry laboratory sequence (CHEM 222L/223L).
courses.requirements: Prerequisites: By course placement. This laboratory class is intended to accompany CHEM 1700 only and may not be taken by any student unless they are either enrolled in CHEM 1700 concurrently or have already completed CHEM 1700 and have not in either case completed a higher numbered Chemistry laboratory class,

courses.title: Clinical Database Management Systems and Ontologies
courses.description: This course introduces database and ontology in the clinical/public health domain. It reviews how data and information are generated in clinical/public health settings. It introduces different approaches to representing, modeling, managing, querying, and integrating clinical/public health data. In terms of database technologies, the course describes two main approaches—SQL database and non-SQL (NoSQL) database—and shows how these technologies can be used to build electronic health records (EHR), data repositories, and data warehouses. In terms of ontologies, it discusses how ontologies are used in connecting and integrating data with machine-readable knowledge. The course reviews the major theories, methods, and tools for the design and development of databases and ontologies. It also includes clinical/public health use cases demonstrating how databases and ontologies are used to support clinical/public health research.
courses.requirements: Prerequisite: CPSC 223 or permission of the instructors. The general expectation to obtain instructor permission is that students have basic command of the Python programming language sufficient to pass CPSC 223 or the equivalent.

courses.title: Directed Studies: Historical and Political Thought
courses.description: A study of works of primary importance to political thought and intellectual history. Focus on the role of ideas in shaping events, institutions, and the fate of the individual. In the fall term, Herodotus, Thucydides, Plato, Aristotle, Augustine, and Aquinas. In the spring term, Machiavelli, Hobbes, Locke, Rousseau, Burke, Tocqueville, Emerson, Marx, Nietzsche, and Arendt.
courses.requirements: You must be an admitted student of the Directed Studies program in order to register for this course

courses.title: Directed Studies: Philosophy
courses.description: An examination of major figures in the history of Western philosophy with an aim of discerning characteristic philosophical problems and their interconnections. Emphasis on Plato and Aristotle in the fall term. In the spring term, modern philosophers include Descartes, Berkeley, Hume, Kant, and Nietzsche.

courses.title: School Health Clinical Practice
courses.description: This course is designed to provide an opportunity to develop an advanced practice nursing role in the school setting. Experience is in a school-based clinic where the student provides primary and episodic care to the client population, participates in health education, as well as consults and collaborates with other health and education personnel in the school and community. Required of all pediatric nurse practitioner primary care students in the second term of the first year of specialization or the first term of the final year. Ninety hours of clinical practice.
courses.classnotes: Course meets in room 01105.

courses.title: Science, Technology and Research Scholars (STARS) I program
courses.description:
The STARS I program is affiliated with the Yale College Dean's Office and is run by the Science and Quantitative Reasoning Office. The program promotes retention and success in STEM for first-year students interested in a STEM major, but might be underprepared in STEM classes and have had limited exposure to research. The program provides peer-mentoring and workshops throughout the academic year to foster growth, success, and retention in STEM. Students meet with faculty and alumni to learn about career paths, and meet with fellow students to learn about research and STEM journeys at Yale. The program cultivates a welcoming and inclusive community, fostering friendships, camaraderie, and cohort-building.

This course can not be applied toward the 36-course-credit requirement for the Yale Bachelor's degree and is graded pass/fail.
courses.requirements: Enrollment for accepted students only. Contact Alexia Belperron (alexia.belperron@yale.edu) for application information.

courses.title: Elementary Czech I
courses.description: This course aims to develop basic proficiency in understanding, reading, speaking and writing the Czech language. Through work with a textbook, workbook, audio files and a broad range of authentic printed and online Czech language materials, students should develop mastery of the most essential vocabulary and grammatical structures necessary for basic communication in Czech and for laying a solid foundation for further study of the language. Students should reach out to sci-cls@yale.edu if they have questions about the course.

courses.title: Elementary Czech II
courses.description: Continuation of CZEC 110. This course aims to expand basic proficiency in understanding, reading, speaking, and writing the Czech language. The course works through a selection of dialogues, texts and exercises to develop mastery of the most essential idiomatic vocabulary and grammatical structures necessary for basic communication in Czech and for laying a solid foundation for further study of the language.
courses.requirements: Prerequisite: CZEC 110 or equivalent. Course taught through distance learning using videoconferencing technology from Columbia University. Enrollment limited; interested students should e-mail sci-cls@yale.edu for more information.

courses.title: The Russian Lyric
courses.description: This graduate seminar offers an introduction to the study of nineteenth- and twentieth-century Russian-language lyric poetry. Topics of discussion will include Russian poetry in comparative contexts; the lyric and the nation or empire; modes of reading and theories of the lyric; performance and dissemination; reading cultures and imagined communities; total art and lyric form; medium and other media; aesthetic autonomy and political engagement; and other topics . Our approach will emphasize form and medium as well as context and consequence; our weekly practices will involve close reading, theoretical reframing, original research, and ongoing collaborative participation and presentations. We will pay particular attention to the legacies of Romanticism—and we will begin with Adorno’s insight from the 1950s as inspiration: that the task of critical thought arising from poetry is "to discover how the entirety of a society, as a unity containing contradictions, appears in a work; in which respects the work remains true to its society, and in which it transcends that society.

courses.title: ISM Colloquium
courses.description: The Institute of Sacred Music Colloquium is central to the purpose of the Institute and to the faculty’s involvement in, and personal attention to, how ISM students are trained. Colloquium is the meeting ground for all Institute students and faculty, the place where we study together, grapple with major issues, and share our work as students of sacred music, worship, and the arts. Taken for .5 credits per term, Colloquium meets every Wednesday from 3:30 until 5 p.m., with informal discussion from 5 to 5:30 p.m. ISM students from the two partner schools of Music and Divinity collaborate on a presentation to be given in their final year. The course is divided into two term-long parts, with responsibility for the fall term resting primarily with the faculty and outside presenters, and for the spring term primarily with the students.

courses.title: Advanced Topics in Deep Learning: General-Purpose Sequence Processing
courses.description: This graduate seminar introduces participants to general-purpose sequence processing and related topics in deep learning. Sequence-processing neural networks are ubiquitous and versatile tools. Whether you are interested in building chatbots that can hold natural conversations with humans, robots that can shop for groceries in the real world, or computational models of memory in the brain, a sequence model may serve as a fundamental component of such systems. Furthermore, a deep understanding of sequence processing opens the door to other frontier challenges in deep learning, including recurrent reasoning ("thinking" as sequence processing) and meta-learning ("learning" as sequence processing). This course familiarizes participants with both state-of-the-art and historically important sequence-model architectures, as well as related open research questions in deep learning. Participants develop the skills needed to critically read and evaluate research papers in these areas and to formulate their own ideas for advancing these research frontiers or applying these concepts to their domains of interest.
courses.requirements: Prerequisite: Basic knowledge of machine learning and deep learning. Familiarity with neural networks and gradient-based optimization is expected. Prior exposure to sequence models is useful but not required.

courses.title: Senior Research
courses.description: Individual two-term laboratory research projects under the supervision of a faculty member. For MCDB seniors only. Students are expected to spend ten to twelve hours per week in the laboratory, and to make presentations to students and advisers. Written assignments include a short research proposal summary due at the beginning of the first term, a grant proposal due at the end of the first term, and a research report summarizing experimental results due at the end of the second term. Students are also required to present their research in either the fall or the spring term. A poster session is held at the end of the spring term. Students should line up a research laboratory during the term preceding the research. Guidelines for the course may be obtained on the course Canvas site. Written proposals are due by the end of the second week of classes. Fulfills the senior requirement for the B.S. degree if taken in the senior year.

courses.title: Monuments and Memory
courses.description: This graduate seminar examines the monument as a contested medium of collective memory, moving from the classic theorization of lieux de mémoire through the toppled statue, the counter-monument, and the performed or ephemeral memorial. Ranging across the black Atlantic, postcolonial Africa, postsocialist Europe, and the Americas, we ask what monuments do, for whom, and in what temporality—commemorating a past, securing a present, or speculating a future. Each week pairs foundational theory with an artist, site, or public controversy, culminating in the question of what a monument to the future might be.

courses.title: Decentralized Payments, Contracts, and Finance for Humans and AI
courses.description: Blockchains provide a platform for humans to coordinate economic activity without relying on centralized intermediaries. Emerging standards such as EIP-8004 aim to extend these capabilities to autonomous agents, enabling AI systems to transact and coordinate through shared protocols. This introductory course explores such decentralized applications, including tokens, exchanges, lending protocols, stablecoins, oracles, decentralized governance, and emerging standards for AI coordination and interoperability. Students learn system architecture, security intuition, and how to build and debug decentralized applications. Students enrolled in this course work on a semester-long project in which they investigate a technical or societal topic related to the course and present to the class during the final weeks of the semester.

courses.title: Quantum Engineering with Neutral Atoms
courses.description: This is a graduate course on the hardware of quantum computers, with a focus on neutral atoms trapped in optical tweezers. Neutral atoms are one of the most rapidly developing platforms for quantum computing today. The course starts from the basics and builds up the physics needed to understand and design an atom-array quantum computer. Topics include atomic structure, atom–light interaction, laser cooling and trapping, optical tweezers and atom arrays, qubit encodings and coherence, state preparation and readout, single-qubit and two-qubit (Rydberg) gates, gate errors, scaling and architecture, error correction, and analog quantum simulation. The last part of the course looks at the other main hardware platforms (trapped ions, superconducting circuits, photonics, and solid-state spins) using the same set of metrics. By the end, students should be able to read and judge current work on quantum hardware. Intended for graduate students in Applied Physics, Physics, ECE, etc. who are interested in experimental quantum science, quantum information, AMO physics, or quantum optics. Well-prepared advanced undergraduates are also welcome.

Examples of common health problems are: chronic and acute skin conditions, upper respiratory infections, asthma, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, thyroid, diabetes, headaches, and mood disorders. Additionally, students incorporate the primary care foundations of health promotion, risk assessment, disease prevention, and counseling. Required of all women’s health nurse practitioner students. courses.title: Democracy and Development in South Asia
courses.description: This course examines the relationship between political development and economic development in South Asia — a region home to a quarter of the world's population, the largest number of its poor, and some of its most consequential experiments in democratic governance. The course asks: what does it mean for a country to "develop," and what role does politics play in shaping whether and how that happens? To answer this question, the course moves across three parts. It begins with foundational theoretical debates about democracy, regime type, and development — using South Asian cases, as empirical testing grounds for influential macro-theoretical claims. It then turns to the political economy of economic growth: how colonial legacies shaped postcolonial development strategies, how competing ideological frameworks from import-substituting industrialization to neoliberalism to Marxist political economy have informed policy, and what the East Asian and Chinese experiences suggest by comparison. In the final third of the course, the focus shifts from aggregate growth to its distributional consequences — examining poverty, caste, health, education, gender, the environment, migration, and conflict as dimensions of development that GDP cannot capture. Throughout, the course interweaves broad theoretical frameworks with empirical treatments of specific South Asian countries, challenging students to use regional experience to assess, interrogate, and where necessary problematize influential ideas from comparative development studies.

courses.title: Life in Motion: Ecological and Evolutionary Physiology
courses.description: Physiology is the study of the functions that organisms perform and how they use those functions to interact with the environment. To survive, grow, and reproduce, all organisms must acquire energy and avoid conditions that exceed their physiological limits. These interactions all involve motion—ions traveling across membranes, muscle fibers twitching, respiration, and locomotion, to name a few. In this course, we tackle physiological processes from both "bottom up" and "top down" approaches, with integration among these dimensions, to extract general physiological rules of life. Then, we link our discoveries to the broader context of ongoing global change, and consider whether and how organisms can physiologically respond to contemporary selective pressures. While the course focuses heavily on animal physiology, plants, fungi, and microbes are also featured.
courses.requirements: Prerequisites: BIOL 1010, 1020, 1030, 1040, and CHEM 1610, or permission of the instructor.

courses.title: National Security Strategy in Latin America: The Return of Gunboat Diplomacy
courses.description: US foreign policy in Latin America and the Western Hemisphere is undergoing a rapid radical ideological transformation. We explore the divergence between theory and actual reality on the ground. Democracy in Latin America has been a defining hemispheric principle for more than 200 years. The United States issued the Monroe Doctrine to protect the nascent independent republics of the hemisphere. What does the Trump Administration’s new national security strategy (NSS) doctrine mean for US national interests and how is it being applied in the region? Are there alternatives to intervention in national elections, US boat strikes in the Caribbean, and a new economic colonialism? Can we restore democracy in Venezuela? What are the policy tradeoffs between economic recovery, stability, and political transition? Will Cuba be invaded? Is there a viable pathway for reform in Cuba without violent confrontation? What will happen in Brazil’s October presidential election, the continent’s largest democracy? Can Colombia stop the flow of cocaine to the US?  Are human rights once again under siege across the region? This course develops policy recommendations for how US policy makers can design a more effective role for the United States in the region. Understanding the history of US engagement in Latin America is critical to identifying new opportunities for political and economic development throughout the Western Hemisphere in the twenty-first century. We critically analyze whether the Trump Administration NSS can address the current realities regional governments are facing from emerging demographic, political, and economic trends in their societies. Underlying every topic is a review of the United States’ role in contributing to events.

courses.title: Principles of Pediatric Care for Children and Youth with Developmental/Intellectual Disabilities
courses.description: This course introduces students to the principles of advanced practice primary care of children and youth with developmental and intellectual disabilities. Using an ecobiodevelopmental framework, the course examines the various clinical presentations and underpinnings, challenges, and joys inherent in caring for this population. It explores many of the medical-, school-, and community-based interventions and therapies that optimize development and emphasizes the necessary collaboration with these colleagues. Importantly, the course offers a lens into the lived experience of children, youth, and their caregivers across the continuum of early childhood, school-aged, and adolescent development. The course touches on the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act, both its facets and implications, as well as the barriers to realization and access to care. Experiential in design, the course blends lecture, direct observation, and reflective process to emphasize relational care and clinical humility while equipping nurse practitioners with a deeper and broader clinical toolkit to meaningfully support these patients and their families.

courses.title: ACE Praticum Elective
courses.description:
The ACE Practicum Elective provides a structured, mentored experience for masters students to receive academic credit for year-long Associate Course Educator (ACE) work focused on scaling high-quality clinical reasoning. Traditionally, the ACE role has been reserved for senior medical students, but other interested MHS students (residents, fellows, and practicing clinicians) can participate with permission from the course director. The elective formalizes participation and contributions across four ACE expectation domains: teaching, curriculum development, scholarship, and citizenship. The practicum includes deliberate practice in teaching clinical reasoning, participation in faculty development and quality assurance (direct observation and structured teaching exercises), development of implementable curricular products, and completion of a dissemination-oriented scholarship deliverable.


ACE Program Expectations (Four-Fold)


1) Teaching


•Approximately 12.5 hours per credit per semester devoted to teaching activities (preparation + delivery + debrief), spread across various in-person and online teaching opportunities.


•Participate in direct observation(s) of teaching by the course director with feedback and at least one observed structured teaching exercise. These observations can be done in real time or via recordings of teaching sessions.


2) Curriculum Development


•Lead or co-lead development or continuation of at least one medical education project/thread, often in the form of a curriculum or teaching innovation.


3) Scholarship


•Submit at least one scholarship deliverable, such as:


•Conference presentation (poster/oral), and/or


•Manuscript (draft suitable for submission; submission preferred when feasible)


4) Citizenship


•Participate in colleagues’ projects as needed and contribute to a collaborative learning culture.


•Attend at least monthly ACE meetings when schedule permitting, where upcoming classes and initiatives are discussed.


•Participate in relevant faculty development workshops and program activities.


Meetings with the Faculty Elective Director:


The ACE will meet with the Faculty Elective Director three times during the elective:


The dates of these sessions should be decided on and scheduled within the first month of the elective. The first should take place within two months of starting the elective. The last should be close to the end of the course. The first two meetings will involved the faculty director direct observation of the tutor’s interaction with the students. The third meeting will include:


1)Debriefing on the entire course


2)Discussion of ACE’s OSTE report


3)Student feedback given to tutor throughout the course

courses.title: Theology and Desire
courses.description: This seminar invites students to critically reflect on theology and desire. We study the relationship between desiring God and desiring neighbor. We begin with culture, desire, use, and commodity. We progress through creation into theologies of marriage, procreation, celibacy, and sodomy. Then, we pursue God up the mountain, where language slips away. Back on the ground, we look around with blinking eyes to ask what theologies of desire have to say now, and where they might lead us. Students encounter a breadth of texts—including recent theology, early Christian writing, gay/queer theory, and memoir—with a particular focus on gay/queer sexuality. Different texts may be uncomfortable for different students: some are quite confessional, some are sexually explicit, some restrict sexuality. In this seminar, we embrace those moments graciously as we encourage each other to ask, "How do desires for God and neighbor interrupt and intensify one another? How do they inflect relational forms, communities, and languages? Can we name desire’s orientations and disorientations in ways that grasp and expand Christian thought and life today?" This course is fitting for students new to theology and those more acquainted.

courses.title: The Dinosaur-Bird Transition: An Anatomical Approach
courses.description: The evolutionary assembly of the bird body was first one of the deepest mysteries and is now one of the greatest stories in the history of life—a story whose telling owes much to work done at Yale and to evidence in the form of fossils in the collection of the Yale Peabody Museum. In this specimen-based seminar, we trace the anatomical modernization of birds from the basal reptilian divergence to Aves, the crown clade. To do so, we employ a regional approach so as to optimize our comparative understanding of the avian form, part by part. Each session after the organizational meeting begins with a short lecture on the relevant body region and its evolutionary transformations on the avian line, with special attention to "soft" anatomy, especially muscular anatomy, in addition to skeleton, and with some consideration of development. We then discuss one or two short publications on the subject and will spend the remainder of our class time in examination of Yale Peabody Museum specimens that document the origin of birds from nonavian dinosaurs, cross-referencing them with a current phylogenetic matrix of dinosaurs including birds. Course credit for attendance and participation and for leading discussion of one or more publications. Meeting time and place to be decided on the basis of schedules of interested students. Undergraduates can enroll with permission of instructor.

courses.title: Is That Racist?: Theory and Methods for Diagnosing and Demonstrating Racism
courses.description: How do we know when something is racist? And how do we prove it to those who are skeptical? This course is designed to allow students to go beyond armchair pontificating about racism by exploring a broad range of ways social theorists have defined the term and methods they have used to demonstrate it. Together, we have the opportunity to read, critique, and synthesize scholarship from across disciplines, with the goal of refining our own definition of the term. To accomplish this, we examine the stakes of calling something racist, who benefits and who suffers from a given definition, and how racism functions across contexts (mostly) within the United States. We also learn about popular methods for demonstrating that an idea, feeling, behavior, person, or institution is racist and evaluate how evidence about racism (or lack thereof) can obscure a diagnosis of racism—or lead to an erroneous one. Throughout the course, we take opportunities to translate the theoretical and methodological lessons we learn to the world we live in today, from popular culture to dinner table conversations.

courses.title: Working Group on Globalization and Culture
courses.description: A continuing yearlong collective research project, a cultural studies "laboratory." The group, drawing on several disciplines, meets regularly to discuss common readings, develop collective and individual research projects, and present that research publicly. The general theme for the working group is globalization and culture, with three principal aspects: (1) the globalization of cultural industries and goods, and its consequences for patterns of everyday life as well as for forms of fiction, film, broadcasting, and music; (2) the trajectories of social movements and their relation to patterns of migration, the rise of global cities, the transformation of labor processes, and forms of ethnic, class, and gender conflict; (3) the emergence of and debates within transnational social and cultural theory. The specific focus, projects, and directions of the working group are determined by the interests, expertise, and ambitions of the members of the group, and change as its members change.

courses.title: Histories of American Reproductive Health, Rights, and Activism from 1800
courses.description: Are all politics reproductive politics? This course traces the reproductive history of the United States from the early nineteenth century to the present day. Questions about reproduction–and about not reproducing–are deeply tied to questions of gendered and racial rights; of bodily autonomy; of American expansion and empire; and of who counts as a citizen, or even as a human being. In the past few years, we’ve encountered new stories about everything from new and restrictive abortion laws, to immigrant woman who were sterilized without their consent, to new technologies in male birth control, to the inequitable childcare burden that falls to women during times of hardship, to the racist roots of foster care and residential school systems. In this course, we come to understand the historical changes in American reproduction to better understand the complicated roots of our current moment. By analyzing articles in newspapers and scientific journals, advertisements, film, patient and physician narratives, and exhibitions and material culture, students will understand reproduction as a site for empowerment and activism, as a site of medical professionalization, and as a site of health disparity. We examine reproduction capaciously, including pregnancy and childbirth, birth control and abortion, assistive reproductive technologies, and adoption and foster care. Our analysis is intersectional, and we consider what different identities meant for reproduction historically, as well as in our current moment.

courses.title: Economics for Global Affairs
courses.description: This core course introduces students to the critical issues facing the global economy today. One of the main goals of the course is to practice how to use measurement and economic frameworks to analyze current events. The course teaches students how to apply economic reasoning to policy issues in the real world building on the concepts covered in the first-semester economics course and new concepts presented in the course.  We use these frameworks to understand questions such as: Why do some countries richer than others? How much inequality is, and should we worry about it?, How are wages and interest rates determined? How do countries conduct fiscal and monetary policy to smooth the business cycle? What determines the gains from international trade and migration? Graded only, sat/unsat option is not permissible.
courses.classnotes: Core Jackson School course open to Jackson School MPP students only.

courses.title: Comparative Politics for Global Affairs
courses.description: Economics can tell us with increasing precision what policies maximize growth, welfare, and productivity. But how are policies actually made? Why are so many poor policies adopted and good ones foregone? In this course students investigate how government organization and the structure of political competition shape the conditions for better and worse economic policy making across a range of economic policies including macroeconomic policy, corporate and financial regulation, industrial policy, and trade. Students consider these policy areas in democratic and nondemocratic regimes, and in developed and developing countries. Graded only, sat/unsat option is not permissible.
courses.classnotes: Core Jackson School course open to Jackson MPP students only.

courses.title: Artificial Intelligence, Emerging Technologies, and National Power II
courses.description: Part II of this two-term course continues to examine how artificial intelligence (AI) has the potential to alter the fundamental building blocks of world order. Machines capable of sophisticated information processing, towards the frontier of autonomy, pose tremendous opportunities for economic growth and societal well-being. Yet the potential risks also are extraordinary. How can we build AI systems that are reliable, transparent, safe, scalable, and aligned with human values? Following an introduction to AI and survey of current research challenges, the seminar focuses on seven core areas where AI and emergent technologies already pose significant security concerns: (1) lethal autonomous weapons and the nature of conflict, (2) disinformation and the future of democracy, (3) competition and conflict in U.S.-China relations, (4) AI ethics and safety, (5) AI governance, (6) nanotechnology and quantum computing, and (7) outer-space development. For each of these sub-units, the goal is to equip aspiring leaders with requisite technical fluency, and to bridge the divide across the law, technology, and policy communities at Yale.

courses.title: Manipulation in the Age of AI
courses.description: The aim of this course is to equip students with an applied understanding of the emerging threats and potential solutions to AI-powered manipulation. Grounded in historical context, the course takes an interdisciplinary lens to the evolution of manipulative media and propaganda from the Roman empire to the near future. The consumption and production of misinformation is first studied at the level of the individual producer and consumer using recent anthropological research. Students test out cutting edge techniques from psychology (inoculation theory) and behavioral economics (nudge theory) to resist the effects of manipulation and learn how these are being applied in new technologies and regulations. Subsequent classes survey the larger economic and political forces shaping the supply and demand of misinformation, including government regulatory efforts on AI and misinformation, plus the "dark web" of unmoderated online platforms. To understand the power of new generative AI tools firsthand, students take a hands-on approach to experiment with both generative AI creation and detection.

courses.title: Artificial Intelligence, Ethics, and Society
courses.description: This seminar examines the development and implementation of artificial intelligence technologies across a broad array of social contexts, incorporating historical, cultural, economic, legal, and political perspectives. The course provides an in-depth study of contemporary AI, from its historical development and varied definitions to current issues, emphasizing the relationship between power dynamics and ethical considerations. After establishing a foundation in theories and the study of ethics and power, the course delves into diverse aspects of AI, including the implications of human labor and material infrastructures in the development of the technology, concerns related to bias and discrimination, and its impacts on the environment. The concluding module applies these discussions to real-world scenarios, exploring how to address ethical and societal issues through legal and human rights frameworks, governance and regulation, and grassroots initiatives. This course is ideal for both computer science and engineering students seeking a socio-humanistic perspective on artificial intelligence, and humanities and social sciences students interested in the societal implications of AI.
courses.classnotes: IMPORTANT: This is a very popular course with more than one hundred applicants last semester. When applying, please indicate your background and why you are interested in the course.

courses.title: Digital War
courses.description: From drones and autonomous robots to algorithmic warfare, virtual war gaming, and data mining, digital war has become a key pressing issue of our times and an emerging field of study. This course provides a critical overview of digital war, understood as the relationship between war and digital technologies. Modern warfare has been shaped by digital technologies, but the latter have also been conditioned through modern conflict: DARPA (the research arm of the US Department of Defense), for instance, has innovated aspects of everything from GPS to stealth technology, personal computing, and the Internet. Shifting beyond a sole focus on technology and its makers, this class situates the historical antecedents and present of digital war within colonialism and imperialism. We investigate the entanglements between technology, empire, and war, and examine how digital war—also sometimes understood as virtual or remote war—has both shaped the lives of the targeted and been conditioned by imperial ventures. We consider visual media, fiction, art, and other works alongside scholarly texts to develop a multidisciplinary perspective on the past, present, and future of digital war.

courses.title: Ethnography & Journalism
courses.description: While each is loathed to admit it, journalism and ethnography are cousins in some respects interested in (albeit distinct) modes of storytelling, translation, and interpretation. This methods course considers these shared grounds to launch a cross-comparative examination. What can the practies of each field and method—journalism and ethnography—tell us about the other? How do journalists and ethnographers engage ideas about the truth? What can they learn from each other? Students spend the first four weeks studying journalistic methods and debates before shifting to ethnographic discussions, and finally, comparative approaches to writing; data and evidence; experience and positionality.

courses.title: Histories and Methods of American Studies
courses.description: Intended primarily for juniors in American Studies, this course serves as both an introduction to American Studies and preparation for senior essays/projects in the major. It explores the histories of American Studies as a field and examines commonly used research methods. Students chart their own entry points and pathways through American Studies by completing scaffolded assignments that draw on both primary and secondary sources. Secondary objectives include strengthening relationships with American Studies faculty and peers and deepening engagement with the undergraduate American Studies program at Yale.

courses.title: Labor and Technology Studies
courses.description: This seminar is structured as a laboratory for the study of labor and technology, focusing on recent transformations driven by the digital economy. We draw from several disciplines to analyze readings, conduct scholarly reviews, develop research projects, and discuss various aspects of the academic profession. The topics and discussions are informed by the background and interests of each cohort of students, complementing the instructor’s ongoing research in three areas: the gig economy and the use of labor platforms both locally and internationally, the impacts of artificial intelligence on work and broader policy and governance, and the effects of digital infrastructures on workers and their communities. Permission of the instructor is required to enroll in this seminar. Undergraduates may enroll with the instructor’s permission.

Please email the instructor indicating the project you would like to develop during the semester. Describe your background and your interest in the seminar topics.
Undergraduates can be admitted to this course only if they have an ongoing project with the course instructor. This seminar does not have a YC code and undergraduates should expect graduate-level coursework.

courses.title: Colonial Domesticity and Reproductive Relations
courses.description: In this interdisciplinary seminar, we study the central importance of kinship, family, and domestic labor to the social reproduction of racial colonial processes. Settler colonialism, colonial slavery, overseas empire, and their aftermaths depend not only on the brute force of war, captivity, and occupation; they are also sustained and contested through culture, language, forms of family and household, and the social reproduction of race, gender, intimacy, and filiation. We trace a genealogy of "colonial domesticity" that considers histories of the sexual violation and separation of slave women from their children, compulsory boarding schools for Native Americans, racialized gendered divisions of care labor, transnational Asian adoption, and contemporary migrant detention and family separation; this genealogy also includes alternative forms of kinship, domesticity, generation, and relation. Readings include historical and anthropological studies of colonialism, feminist debates on social reproduction, and literary and visual culture materials by Maria Mies, Ann Laura Stoler, Silvia Federici, Tithi Bhattacharya, Ruha Benjamin, Kalindi Vora, Thavolia Glymph, Saidiya Hartman, Dorothy Roberts, Audra Simpson, Jodi Byrd, Amy Kaplan, Evelyn Nakano Glenn, Laura Briggs, Elizabeth Freeman, Chandan Reddy, Alys Weinbaum, Louise Erdrich, Mary Prince, Toni Morrison, Patricia Powell, Chang-rae Lee, Octavia Butler, and others.

courses.title: Theory of Electromagnetic Waves, Radiation, and Scattering
courses.description: This is a graduate-level course on electromagnetic theory, focusing on electromagnetic wave phenomena in a variety of contexts. Electrostatics and magnetostatics are reviewed briefly and then the full time-dependent Maxwell equations are studied to derive the fundamentals of wave propagation, the wave equation, plane waves, polarization, energy and momentum flow in EM waves, conservation laws, gauge transformation, and Green functions for the wave equations. Dielectric media and Fresnel reflection and refraction, total internal reflection, group velocity, wave packets and dispersion. Beam propagation and gaussian optics, optical birefringence. Waves in confined structures, waveguides, optical fibers, resonant cavities. Radiating sources, electric and magnetic dipolar radiation, multipolar radiation, near and far-field solutions, radiating antennas. Scattering theory, scalar and vector diffraction, Rayleigh scattering, scattering matrix and temporal coupled mode theory, scattering resonances, multiple scattering, systems with gain and lasing. Time permitting: relativistic kinematics, covariance of Maxwell's equations, Lorentz transformation of electric and magnetic fields, relativistic mechanics of charged particles.
courses.requirements: Prerequisites: an undergraduate course on electricity and magnetism and graduate-level vector calculus and differential equations.

courses.title: Modern Topics in Optics and Quantum Electronics
courses.description: This course provides a survey of modern topics involving integrated photonics, optomechanics, nonlinear optics, and laser physics for students interested in contemporary experimental optics research. Subjects include nonlinear wave phenomena, optomechanical interactions, phonon physics, light scattering, light emission and detection, cavities, systems of cavities, traveling-wave devices and interactions, perturbation theory, reciprocal and nonreciprocal systems, parametric interactions, laser oscillators and related technologies. Students are encouraged to explore these and related research topics through independent study and classroom presentations.

courses.title: Circuit Quantum Electrodynamics
courses.description: Circuit quantum electrodynamics, or circuit QED, is the field of quantum optics with microwave photons, and is the basis of most solid-state quantum computing technologies. In the microwave domain, we can engineer the properties of "artificial atoms" constructed from circuits containing Josephson junctions and couple them strongly to stationary photons trapped in a cavity or resonant circuit and to traveling photons in a waveguide or transmission line. With this approach, one can access regions of strong coupling between "light" and "matter" that are not accessible in atomic physics. This course is an introduction to the concepts and techniques of circuit QED, aimed for the beginning graduate student or advanced undergraduate with a solid background in classical electricity and magnetism and also basic quantum mechanics. The course is intended to provide an important base of knowledge that can prepare the student for research in quantum information processing with superconducting circuits. Topics to be covered include the basics of superconducting qubits, the Jaynes-Cummings model and the strong dispersive regime, and the use of light-matter interactions for measurement, control, and quantum computing with quantum circuits. Extra work for graduate students: The last homework set is optional for undergrads and required for grads.
courses.requirements: Prerequisites: one semester QM and one semester E&M at advanced undergrad or higher.

courses.title: Origins and the Search for Life in the Universe
courses.description: Origins of the universe, stars, and planets; evolution of conditions that were conducive to the emergence of life on Earth; leading theories for the origin of life; the discovery of exoplanets; comparison of Earth's solar system with other systems that have been discovered; the possibility of habitable conditions where life might have arisen on other worlds; methods of searching for life elsewhere.
courses.requirements: No prerequisite other than a working knowledge of elementary algebra.

courses.title: Introduction to Cosmology
courses.description: An introduction to modern cosmological theories and observational astronomy. Topics include aspects of special and general relativity; curved space-time; the Big Bang; inflation; primordial element synthesis; the cosmic microwave background; the formation of galaxies; and large-scale structure.
courses.requirements: Prerequisite: a strong background in high school mathematics and physics.

courses.title: Galaxies and Cosmology
courses.description: An intensive introduction to extragalactic astronomy. The structure and contents of galaxies, evolution of galaxies, observational cosmology, and the history of the universe. Students observe a deep-sky object with campus telescopes.
courses.requirements: Prerequisite: a strong background in high school calculus and physics. May not be taken after ASTR 210.

courses.title: Galactic and Extragalactic Astronomy
courses.description: Structure of the Milky Way galaxy and other galaxies; stellar populations and star clusters in galaxies; gas and star formation in galaxies; the evolution of galaxies; galaxies and their large-scale environment; galaxy mergers and interactions; supermassive black holes and active galactic nuclei.
courses.requirements: Prerequisites: MATH 1150, PHYS 2010, and ASTR 2100 or 2200, or equivalents, or with permission of instructor.

courses.title: Scientific Computing in Astrophysics
courses.description: Scientific computer programming in Astrophysics with a focus on the Python Programming language. Algorithms and workflows for reducing and analyzing Astrophysical datasets, both observational and computational. Emphasis is placed on best coding practices, including readability, version control, documentation, and computational efficiency. Weekly lectures, in-depth tutorial/workshops, and invited outside expert guest speakers. Students complete a programming project based on real astrophysical datasets.
courses.requirements: Prerequisite: ASTR 255 or permission of instructor. Some basic programming experience in Python is strongly recommended.

courses.title: Exoplanets
courses.description: Planet formation, exoplanet detection techniques, and the modeling of observations of exoplanet atmospheres. Solar system architecture compared with other planetary systems. From an Earth-centric perspective, habitability factors of rocky planets and the implications for life elsewhere.
courses.requirements: Prerequisites: MATH 120 and PHYS 201 or equivalents, and one astronomy course numbered above 200.

courses.description: The physics of stellar atmospheres and interiors. Topics include the basic equations of stellar structure, nuclear processes, stellar evolution, white dwarfs, and neutron stars.

The basic physical processes underlying the observed high-energy phenomena are also covered.
