courses.description: The course explores foundational topics in behavioral economics and discusses the dominant prescriptive models (which propose what decision makers should do) and descriptive models (which aim to describe what decision makers actually do). The course incorporates perspectives from economics, psychology, philosophy, decision theory, and finance, and engages long-standing debates about rational choice.

courses.title: Foundations of Behavioral Economics
courses.description: The course explores foundational topics in behavioral economics and discusses the dominant prescriptive models (which propose what decision makers should do) and descriptive models (which aim to describe what decision makers actually do). The course incorporates perspectives from economics, psychology, philosophy, decision theory, and finance, and engages long-standing debates about rational choice.

courses.title: Financial Econometrics and Machine Learning
courses.description: This is a course in advanced statistical methods for finance including econometrics, machine learning, and artificial intelligence. The applications of these methods focus on topics in empirical asset pricing including return prediction, risk modeling, portfolio choice, and factor modeling, among others. The goal of the course is to build a state-of-the-art statistical skill set for empirical asset pricing and practical asset management. Must be taken along with MGMT 7206/ECON 6677, Financial Econometrics and Machine Learning.

courses.title: Primary Care of Children II Clinical Practice: B
courses.description: This course provides clinical experience in well child-care and management of common pediatric problems in a variety of primary care settings. Students provide primary health care, acute care and beginning case management for pediatric patients in the context of their families. Required for all pediatric nurse practitioner students. One hundred sixty-six hours in primary care and fourteen hours clinical conference.
courses.requirements: Prerequisite: completion of the GEPN program or RN status.

courses.title: Psychotherapeutic Interventions I: Fundamentals and Individual Psychotherapy
courses.description: This course examines the theory and practice of individual psychotherapeutic interventions across the lifespan. Students develop foundational knowledge and skills to build effective therapeutic relationships. The course provides an overview of major psychotherapy theories and, through case formulation, students begin to apply these theories to clinical practice in ways that align with client preferences, presenting concerns, and biopsychosocial factors. Ethical and legal standards in psychotherapy, along with the role of psychotherapy in PMHNP practice, are also examined.
courses.requirements: Prerequisite: completion of (or concurrent enrollment in): NURS 6000/H, NURS 6010/H, NURS 6020/H, NURS 7606/H, NURS 7625/H, NURS 7771/H.

courses.title: Psychopharmacologic Interventions I: Foundations in Psychopharmacology
courses.description: This is the first of two courses preparing the PMHNP student to prescribe psychotropic medication to treat mental disorders in individuals across the lifespan. Students gain foundational knowledge of the major classes of psychotropic medication, the disorders they treat, and the neurobiology necessary to understand the actions of drugs on the brain. Students learn the role of the advanced practice provider in prescriptive practice, incorporating evidence-based, person-centered care. Thirty hours.
courses.requirements: Prerequisite: completion (or concurrent enrollment in) NURS 6000, NURS 6010, NURS 6020, NURS 7606, NURS 7625, and NURS 7771.

courses.title: Psychiatric-Mental Health Clinical Practice II
courses.description: This is the second in a series of four clinical practica. Each seminar is designed to build up the requisite knowledge, skills, and attitude (KSA) of PMHNP practice to a targeted level of competency, which is evaluated in the clinical setting by the preceptor’s ability to entrust the student with specific core aspects of PMHNP practice. In this second clinical practicum, emphasis is on direct supervision and close preceptor collaboration. Students perform core psychiatric tasks—including history taking, mental status examinations, initial assessments, and participation in therapeutic sessions (e.g., co-facilitating group therapy)—alongside their supervisors. Entrustment of PMHNP activities and KSA is expected to be moderate, with preceptor-observed and joint practice the norm. Experiences can include working with individuals, groups, and families across the lifespan. Students use the clinical case conference format to integrate and apply clinical skills. Students must complete 195 requisite clinical hours to complete this course and attend fifteen hours of seminar.
courses.requirements: Prerequisite: previous completion of, or concurrent enrollment in, NURS 6000/H, NURS 6010/H, NURS 6020/H, NURS 7606/H, NURS 7625/H, and NURS 7771/H.

courses.title: Psychotherapeutic Interventions III: Complex Cases and Systems of Care
courses.description: This is the third course in a series of three courses that examine the practice and application of psychotherapy across the lifespan. This course builds on knowledge gained in courses NURS 7615 and NURS 7715, Psychotherapeutic Interventions I and II. The focus of this course is to synthesize psychotherapeutic principles and biopsychosocial and cultural factors within specific populations. Psychotherapeutic treatment of complex cases within systems of care are addressed. Advanced topics including management of comorbidities and specialized therapeutic treatment modalities across the lifespan are covered. Analysis of health-equity and health-systems factors impacting psychotherapeutic care delivery are examined.
courses.requirements: Prerequisites: successful completion of NURS 7615 and NURS 7715.

courses.title: Psychiatric-Mental Health Clinical Practice IV
courses.description: This is the fourth course in a series of four that aim to develop the clinical and leadership skills required for advanced psychiatric mental health nursing practice. Emphasis is placed on incorporating emerging evidence and innovation into clinical decision making, ordering and documenting diagnostic and screening tests, evaluating care outcomes, and adjusting the plan of care with the interprofessional team. Students are expected to foster community partnerships, participate in system-level change initiatives, determine population priorities for care, and design policy to impact health equity. Students expand their leadership skills by engaging in professional organization and professional service opportunities. In their clinical setting, students collaboratively provide care for individuals, groups, and families for complex presentations (more than two diagnoses) involving multiple systems engagement. Students are assigned to psychiatric clinical placements to align with competency development, previous clinical experiences, and interests. Students use the clinical case conference format to integrate and apply clinical skills. Clinical case conference meets weekly; clinical practicum hours are 225 for this course.
courses.requirements: Prerequisite: Psychiatric-Mental Health Clinical Practice III.

courses.title: D.N.P. Project: Evidence-Based Practice Change
courses.description: Students apply relevant knowledge to an evidence-based, yearlong experience culminating in a final D.N.P. project manuscript, which will be submitted for publication. The D.N.P. project includes critical review and integration of relevant literature/research that provides support of the identified population-based health issue or problem, as well as at least one policy and/or evidence-based strategy that has the potential to address that health issue or problem. Required of all D.N.P. students in the final year.

courses.title: Leadership Immersion Practicum
courses.description: The Leadership Immersion is a yearlong, mentored experience in which students apply relevant knowledge to an evidence-based experience culminating in a final D.N.P. project in NURS 9990/NURS 9991. Students employ effective communication and collaboration skills to influence improved health care quality and safety and to negotiate successful changes in care delivery processes within and/or across health and health care systems and organizations. Students complete the immersion under guidance of the site mentor, who will be a member of the nursing faculty D.N.P. project adviser/committee under the leadership of the D.N.P. project chair and the D.N.P. director. Required of all D.N.P. students in the final year. 225 practicum hours.
courses.requirements: Prerequisites: successful completion of all required theoretical and D.N.P. project courses as well as an approved D.N.P. project proposal.

courses.title: The Business of Health Care
courses.description: This course focuses on the synthesis of theoretical and practical principles of economics, financial decision-making, and business in health care systems and organizations. Principles of finance and fiscal management are used to analyze revenue streams, payer sources, reimbursement, and value-based payment models. Budgeting for both short-term operations and long-term strategy is applied to current and emerging health care delivery models. Ethical responsibilities in financial and business decision-making are emphasized, including delivery models focused on population health equity. Business communications and negotiations are practiced and critiqued. Required of all D.N.P. students in the second year.
courses.requirements: Prerequisites: NURS 9670 and NURS 9690.

courses.title: Clinical Inquiry Seminar I
courses.description: This seminar for the Clinical D.N.P. student supports the initial development of the clinical area of inquiry separate from the D.N.P. project proposal. Topics discussed in the seminar include: the structure and process of clinical knowledge development and translation, assessing existing evidence in relationship to current clinical practices and processes of change, identification of factors to ensure effective clinical implementation, and approaches to clinical scholarship development including communication and expression.  Seminar outcomes include an individualized Clinical Area of Inquiry Plan, summary of inquiry activities completed, and a project proposal identifying and clarifying the focus and site for the D.N.P. project as separate from the area of clinical inquiry. This course is required for all first-year Clinical D.N.P. students.
courses.requirements: Prerequisite: NURS 9600.

courses.title: Quality and Safety in Health Care Organizations
courses.description: This course provides an overview of theoretical principles and concepts essential to assessing, designing, implementing, and evaluating population-based health projects within and across the health system and other organizations. In this course, students critically examine change, decision-making, evaluation, and management-related theories as a foundation for project planning, implementation, and evaluation of an evidence-based improvement project. Students identify and develop a theory-based project derived from an integrated synthesis of the literature. Students also identify appropriate software, tools, and communication techniques essential for leading an interprofessional team from inception to completion of the project within and across health care systems or other organizations. The tools and processes learned in this course will support work toward the subsequent D.N.P. final project. Required of all D.N.P. students in the first year.

courses.title: DNP Project Seminar I
courses.description: In this first of two project-proposal seminars, students develop Part 1 of their project proposal. Part 1 of the proposal includes relevant background and rationale, systematic evidence assessment and discussion, and presentation of the project management model and supporting frameworks as well as an organizational assessment. Appropriate evidence-based methods and tools are used to build this section of the proposal. All relevant appendices are included with specific attention to evidence mapping, search strategy, project model, and organizational analysis. Required for all post-master’s leadership D.N.P. students in their first year. Thirty hours.
courses.requirements: Prerequisites: NURS 9570; NURS 9630.

courses.title: D.N.P. Project: Part 1
courses.description: In this first of two project proposal seminars, students develop Part 1 of their project proposal. Part 1 of the proposal includes relevant background and rationale, systematic evidence assessment and discussion, and presentation of the project management model and supporting frameworks as well as an organizational assessment. Appropriate evidence-based methods and tools are used to build this section of the proposal. All relevant appendices are included with specific attention to evidence mapping, search strategy, project model, and organizational analysis. Required for all post-master’s clinical D.N.P. students in their first year. Thirty hours.
courses.requirements: Prerequisites: NURS 9570; NURS 9630.

courses.title: Clinical D.N.P. Practicum I
courses.description: This course is the first in a series of three Clinical D.N.P. practica in which students gain experience in preparing for, developing, implementing, evaluating, and disseminating their D.N.P. projects. In this first practicum course, students begin to engage and work with experts in the healthcare systems and agencies where they will conduct their projects. Students work with their outside experts and designated agency personnel to identify the systems opportunities and challenges related to project implementation and develop a plan to address them. This practicum prepares D.N.P. students for the systems interactions involved in planning and executing clinical projects. The expected outcomes are: (1) an agreement with the agency for D.N.P. project implementation, (2) engagement and planning activities with agency personnel involved in requisite protocols for project implementation, and (3) development of a relationship with an external expert. The expected outcomes are a signed agreement from their external expert, and a finalized written plan for D.N.P. project implementation. This contains the plan for meeting all requisite protocols required by the agency, including appropriate human subject protocols. This course is required for all Clinical D.N.P. students after successful completion of the year-two fall term.

courses.title: Health Care Policy, Politics, and Process
courses.description: This course provides an overview of past and current health policy and provides the student with the opportunity to critically analyze basic concepts, principles and consequences of policy options for achieving selected health services goals across the spectrum of healthcare. It is built upon the understanding that health care delivery is the transformation of health science into health service. Policy, politics, and processes occur at the national, state, and local levels. Because the course has a primary focus on national healthcare policy, students increase their aptitude in policy, politics, and process to shape improvements. The class tracks and analyzes contemporary legislative and regulatory proposals, processes, and relevant materials to inform discussion. Required for all post-master’s D.N.P. students in their second year. Forty-five hours.
courses.requirements: Prerequisite: all first-year courses.

courses.title: D.N.P. Project Proposal Writing Seminar 2
courses.description: This writing seminar for D.N.P. students supports the finalization and refinement of Part 2 of the D.N.P. proposal. The primary seminar outcome is a finalized Part 2 section of the D.N.P. project proposal which evidences critical thinking and synthetic doctoral level writing as well as precision in writing project methods. This seven-and-a-half-hour seminar provides the student with additional mentoring in the creation of a well-structured methods section and integrated D.N.P. project proposal. This course is required for all second-year Healthcare Leadership, Systems, and Policy Program D.N.P. students.
courses.requirements: Prerequisites: NURS 9890 (01), NURS 9891 (01), NURS 9900 (01).

courses.title: D.N.P. Project Proposal Writing Seminar 2
courses.description: This writing seminar for D.N.P. students supports the finalization and refinement of Part 2 of the D.N.P. proposal. The primary seminar outcome is a finalized Part 2 section of the D.N.P. project proposal which evidences critical thinking and synthetic doctoral level writing as well as precision in writing project methods. This seven-and-a-half-hour seminar provides the student with additional mentoring in the creation of a well-structured methods section and integrated D.N.P. project proposal. This course is required for all second-year Clinical D.N.P. students.
courses.requirements: Prerequisites: NURS 9890 (02); NURS 9891 (02); NURS 9900 (02).

courses.title: Clinical D.N.P. Practicum III
courses.description: This course is the third and final in a series of three Clinical D.N.P. practica in which students gain experience in preparing for, developing, implementing, evaluating, and disseminating their D.N.P. projects. In this final practicum, students evaluate and disseminate their D.N.P. project implementation findings. They develop a plan with their outside mentors/experts to disseminate D.N.P. project findings to the healthcare system or agency where the project was implemented. This includes recommendations for scaling and sustainability. The expected outcome is completion of the final D.N.P. project phases: evaluation and dissemination. This course is required for all Clinical D.N.P. students after successful completion of fall semester, year three.

courses.title: Clinical Inquiry Seminar III
courses.description: The Clinical Inquiry Seminar III synthesizes the clinical area of inquiry activities identified in NURS 9600 and NURS 9610, Clinical Inquiry Seminar I and II. Seminar discussion examines completion of the D.N.P. essential competencies in understanding and innovating delivery of care in health care systems. Outcomes include integrating focused area of D.N.P. expertise by mapping the clinical focus area competencies to Clinical D.N.P. program projects and experiences. Required of all Clinical D.N.P. students in their final term.

courses.title: Strategies for Land Conservation
courses.description: This course is a capstone seminar in strategies for private land conservation. The course focuses primarily on issues within the U.S., although many of its lessons can be applied in other countries. The course explores the legal and financial tools used by the land conservation community, as well as management techniques for addressing key strategic issues. The course will also provide perspectives and time for reflection on the history and future of the land conservation movement. The primary focus of the course is to provide students with knowledge of the tools of private land conservation and the necessary professional skills to apply those tools. The course relies heavily on guest speakers, all of whom are experts and leaders on the topics on which they present. Many of our in-person guest speakers will also be joining a small group of students for dinner after class. Finally, a key deliverable for the course is working with and completing a clinical project for a land conservation organization Course Application: https://forms.gle/h4tvpANy1EsrKqSE6 (Due December 3rd, 2025) This is a cross-listed School of the Environment course. It will be held at YSE and will follow their academic calendar.

courses.title: Sustainable Business Capstone Consulting Clinic
courses.description: The intended outcome of this course is to provide you with a ‘capstone’ experience; consulting to an organization in its early formative years, confronting real-life challenges at the intersections of starting-up, business strategy, and environmental sustainability; all with regular contact with the Founder/Founding team of an entrepreneurial venture started by recent alumni or current student Founders. The course is designed for you to apply tools and insights gained in this and other courses to a defined project; creating deliverables that will be useful to the entrepreneurs leading their organization. It is designed to help prepare anyone who wishes to become a consultant after graduation; though it is also intended to be useful for those that intend to engage with consultants in their careers post-Yale and may be considering becoming an entrepreneur themselves. In short, there is hopefully something in it for many of you! This course is cross-listed with Environment and will follow their academic calendar. Enrollment by application.

courses.title: Applying a Social Innovation Lens to Social Movements
courses.description: This course applies social innovation tools and approaches to building strategies for social movements. We apply a combination of case-based and open discussion, utilizing tools such as stakeholder mapping, asset mapping, problem characterization, and theory of change. These tools are applied to a set of historical and current social movements to help understand institutional and non-institutional strategies for social change. Discussions blend policy, civic action, grassroots organizing, and innovation.

courses.title: Field Methods
courses.description: Principles of phonetics, phonology, morphology, syntax, and semantics applied to the collection and interpretation of novel linguistic data. Data are collected and analyzed by the class as a group, working directly with a speaker of a relatively undocumented language. Discussion of ethics, linguistic diversity, and endangerment,
courses.requirements: Open to majors and graduate students in Linguistics, and to others with permission of instructor. Students should have taken LING 232 or LING 220 and one other linguistics class.

courses.title: Bioethics Refresher Course
courses.description: The required fourth-year bioethics refresher course runs during the spring semester. This involves both an independent component based around a series of videos on ethics and an in-person discussion component. The requirement is that we have eight hours of in-person instruction time. We have a two-hour component based on video content generated by the BBS and three classroom sessions of two hours each. These sessions are NIH mandated, so please plan to attend.
courses.classnotes:
This course will take place on March 12, March 19, April 2, April 9 @ 3-5pm in TAC N203. 

EXCEPTION: Location for April 2 is TBD.

courses.title: Developing and Writing Fellowship Proposals
courses.description: In this course, students learn how fellowship award review panels are run and what the selection criteria are. The NIH National Research Service Award (NRSA) Fellowship is used as the main framework for learning. Students develop NIH-style Biosketches, learn to generate key points in the NIH Research Training Plan, and learn how to write a Specific Aims page and what to consider for the Project Narrative. Through student-led groups, students learn how to critique Specific Aims pages, with input from instructors, and then develop Project Narratives with specific focuses on effective communication of the underlying hypotheses, impact and significance, and experimental plans.
courses.classnotes: This course will meet in the Summer 2027 on June 7, June 14, June 21, June 28, July 12, July 19 in 100 College St, Room 1167.

courses.title: Foundations of Systems Neuroscience
courses.description: An examination of the neural circuits that subserve sensory, motor, cognitive, and affective function, and their relationships to human disorders. A comparative species approach is used to highlight the evolution of neural circuits and their functions. Required of first-year Neuroscience track students.
courses.classnotes: This course will meet on Tuesdays 2:00-3:30 and Thursdays 2:00-4:00. The location is the Dome Room, which is also called SHM-I 500.

courses.title: Readings in Buddhist Studies
courses.description: This seminar introduces students to Buddhist studies. Exploring scholarship on the Buddhist world, from India to Japan, ranging from the premodern to the modern, the course offers an overview of a thriving scholarly field of study, emphasizing the history of the field, disciplinary expectations and practices that have shaped it, and keystone concerns and emerging questions which animate it. Each week, students read a monograph, write a short review, and engage in seminar discussions with their peers. Primarily designed for graduate students, this course may be used to develop familiarity with a new field of study or to acquire a solid foundation for those preparing for qualifying exams in this this area. Prior familiarity with Buddhism is welcome but not required.

courses.title: Independent Study
courses.description: By arrangement with faculty. If you are a non-European & Russian Studies graduate student, you must seek permission of the DGS of European & Russian Studies.

courses.title: Master’s Thesis
courses.description: By arrangement with faculty.

courses.title: Quantum Studio: Differences, Contingencies, & Entanglements that Matter
courses.description: This course explores the artist’s critical relationship to the environment as mediated by "agential realism" – a framework developed by Karen Barad within physics, a field defined by questioning, experimentation, and conjecture. Due to our inability to visualize four spacetime dimensions (three space and one time), how does physics lend to building an artist’s language when matter and light effectively cease to exist? How does this exploration of nature and reality lend to extending the dimensions for production. By positing the artist’s inquiry within a quantum paradigm, and alternatively, the broader purview of the artist’s perspective into another field of inquiry, the course proposes a "laboratory" format of co-existence wherein research becomes, as the Belgian philosopher Isabelle Stengers writes in Another Science is Possible, "particularly insensitive to the questions posed by reality—not, by casting aside science’s actual claims, rather to retract from binaries of rational/irrational to allow for a generative conversation." For example, how do the study of neutrinos and microbes become entangled with codes of justice, or with speculative imaginings beyond the human. This, to explore the potential in transdisciplinary elaborations on how nature really behaves, in the Kantian sense, as a reflection beyond the limits of reason. By referencing fiction, poetry, art practice and theory, and through immersive laboratory practices in visitations to the Yale Wright Laboratory, this course, developed in conversation with Molly Watts, graduate research fellow in Yale’s Department of Physics, refers to quantum physics as a way to confront the renewed conditions for the possibility of objectivity, the nature of measurement, the nature of nature and meaning, and the relationship between discursive practices and the material world. In addressing the quantum realm of interconnectedness as interpreted by physicists like Niels Bohr and Karen Barad – the entanglement underlying sociocultural phenomena is explored – between matter and meaning, material reality and discourse, to reassess the physical and metaphysical notions that rely on restrictive ideas about the physical world. The course will reference historical and contemporary artworks and art practices in conversation with science – for example, Hilma af Klimt’s early 20th c. work in the relation to the scientific developments in her time around hydrodynamics, machines, physics and astronomy, the mid 21st century critical practices of Robert Smithson, whose interest in the Second Law of Thermodynamics led to an interest to represent an "architecture of entropy" within the dialectical constellation of the site/non-site, and the contemporary practices of Tauba Auerbach who is compelled by the exponential notation in a geometric context. Readings will include Octavia Butler’s Parable of the Sower (1993), as a novel that unfolds as a mirror of the geometric properties of a parabola, the arch shaped curve codified by mathematical language as multiple, overlapping, and intersecting triangles to express the movement of time as a slippage between past, present, future.

courses.title: Principles of Biochemistry II
courses.description: A continuation of MB&B 600 that considers the chemistry and metabolism of nucleic acids, the mechanism and regulation of protein and nucleic acid synthesis, and selected topics in macromolecular biochemistry.

courses.title: Biochemistry and Our Changing Climate
courses.description: Climate change is impacting how cells and organisms grow and reproduce. Imagine the ocean spiking a fever: cold-blooded organisms of all shapes, sizes, and complexities struggle to survive when water temperatures go up two–four degrees. Some organisms adapt to extremes, while others cannot. Predicted and observed changes in temperature, pH, and salt concentration do and will affect many parameters of the living world, from the kinetics of chemical reactions and cellular signaling pathways to the accumulation of unforeseen chemicals in the environment, the appearance and dispersal of new diseases, and the development of new foods. In this course, we approach climate change from the molecular point of view, identifying how cells and organisms―from microbes to plants and animals―respond to changing environmental conditions. To embrace the concept of "one health" for all life on the planet, this course leverages biochemistry, cell biology, molecular biophysics, and genetics to develop an understanding of the impact of climate change on the living world. We consider the foundational knowledge that biochemistry can bring to the table as we meet the challenge of climate change.
courses.requirements: Prerequisites: MB&B 500, MB&B 600, and MB&B 601, or permission of the instructor.

courses.title: Northwest Semitic Inscriptions: Aramaic
courses.description: This two-term course is designed to familiarize students with Aramaic epigraphy from the first millennium BCE. The Aramaic grammar is illustrated through early monumental inscriptions on stones from Anatolia and the abundant papyri of the Persian period from Egypt.

courses.title: Elementary Syriac II
courses.description: Syriac was an Aramaic dialect that developed its own written tradition in the northern Levantine city of Edessa in classical antiquity. This course provides students with a basic working knowledge of the language, namely, the three principal scripts (Estrangela, Serṭo, and "Nestorian"), verbal morphology, and the fundamental rules of syntax. The course completes the introduction to the Syriac language. Extracts of several Syriac texts are studied for purposes of application. At the end of the course, students are able to read, translate, and analyze simple texts.
courses.requirements: Prerequisite: RLST 838 / SMTC 5130.

courses.title: Elementary Italian II
courses.description: Continuation of ITAL 1100.

courses.title: Intensive Elementary Italian
courses.description: An accelerated beginning course in Italian that covers in one term the material taught in ITAL 1101 and 1201. This course meets five times a week for 110 minutes. Admits to ITAL 1302 or 1452.
courses.requirements: Enrollment limited to 15.

courses.title: Dangerous Women: Sirens, Sibyls, Poets and Singers from Sappho through Elena Ferrante
courses.description: Was Sappho a feminist? This course tries to answer that question by analyzing how women’s voices have been appropriated by the literary and cultural canon of the west–and how in turn women writers and readers have reappropriated those voices. Students read a generous amount of literary (and in some cases, musical) works, along with a variety of contemporary theoretical approaches so as to engage in conversation about authorship, classical reception, and materiality. Following an introduction to Greek and Roman texts key for problematic female figures such as sirens and sibyls, we turn to two later historical moments to explore how women artists have both broken out of and used the western canon, redefining genre, content, and style in literary creation writ large. How did Renaissance women such as Laura Cereta, Gaspara Stampa, and Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz fashion themselves as authors in light of the classical sources they had at hand? And once we arrive in the 20th and 21st centuries, how do Sibilla Aleramo, Elsa Morante, Anna Maria Ortese, and Elena Ferrante forge a new, feminist writing via classical, queer and/or animal viewpoints?

courses.title: Algorithms of the Mind
courses.description: This course introduces computational theories of psychological processes, with a pedagogical focus on perception and high-level cognition. Each week students learn about new computational methods grounded in neurocognitive phenomena. Lectures introduce these topics conceptually; lab sections provide hands-on instruction with programming assignments and review of mathematical concepts. Lectures cover a range of computational methods sampling across the fields of computational statistics, artificial intelligence and machine learning, including probabilistic programming, neural networks, and differentiable programming.
courses.requirements: Students must have a fairly strong programming background, ideally in a high-level programming language such as Julia, Python or C++.  (The course will use Julia and Python substantially).  Familiarity with bash scripting and HPC use are desirable.  College-level calculus is required, in addition to some exposure to probability and Bayesian inference, or more broadly (probabilistic) machine learning.

courses.title: Christianity and the Law: The First Millennium
courses.description: Christianity has often been treated as a religion of grace, not law—a contrast often worked out, from the New Testament onward, at the expense of Judaism. Engagement with late antique, medieval, and Byzantine sources, however, yields a far more complicated—and far less antinomian—picture. This seminar attends to developments in legal and religious thought during the first millennium CE, with particular emphasis on Christians’ relationship with law. Three central loci focus on the law of the Hebrew Scriptures, and Christians’ appropriation (and frequently simultaneous rejection) thereof; Christians’ engagement with the laws of their civic environs, including the Roman Empire and its successors, the Sassanid Kingdom, and the Caliphates; and Christians’ own efforts at writing law.

courses.title: Introduction to Computing for Engineers and Scientists
courses.description: An introduction to the use of the C and C++ programming languages and the software packages Mathematica and MATLAB to solve a variety of problems encountered in mathematics, the natural sciences, and engineering. General problem-solving techniques, object-oriented programming, elementary numerical methods, data analysis, and graphical display of computational results.
courses.requirements: Prerequisite: MATH 1120 or equivalent. Recommended preparation: previous coding experience.

courses.title: Multivariable Calculus for Engineers
courses.description: An introduction to multivariable calculus focusing on applications to engineering problems. Topics include vector-valued functions, vector analysis, partial differentiation, multiple integrals, vector calculus, and the theorems of Green, Stokes, and Gauss.
courses.requirements: Prerequisite: MATH 1150 or equivalent.

courses.title: Ordinary and Partial Differential Equations with Applications
courses.description: Basic theory of ordinary and partial differential equations useful in applications. First- and second-order equations, separation of variables, power series solutions, Fourier series, Laplace transforms.
courses.requirements: Prerequisites: ENAS 1510 or MATH 1200 or equivalent, and knowledge of matrix-based operations.

courses.title: History of Knowledge Research Seminar
courses.description: The history of knowledge encompasses the history of the natural and social sciences and humanities, as well as histories of artisanal, bureaucratic, local, indigenous, and other forms of knowledge. It poses questions that cut across these different ways of knowing and, in doing so, often intersects with media studies and the history of education. This seminar guides students through the development of a research paper in the history of knowledge. In the first part of the semester, we read a representative sampling of publications in the field. In the second part, students work independently to develop a research article suitable for submission to a scholarly journal while continuing to meet occasionally in a workshop format.

courses.title: Europe and the World, 1500-1900
courses.description: This course draws on historical sociology and comparative legal history to examine European overseas empires and global ordering between 1500 and 1850. It evaluates theoretical approaches to the study of empires and uses case studies to analyze global processes such as early modern state formation, raiding and captive taking, the rise and rule of trading companies, and the exercise and limits of patrimonial power. Other themes receiving in-depth attention include legal frameworks for imperial-Indigenous and inter-imperial relations, and revolts and rebellions by enslaved and Indigenous peoples. The course is global but not comprehensive in scope, and readings and lectures address problems in both primary and secondary sources.

courses.title: Modes of Performance
courses.description: How do performers make things? How do artists study as they create, and how do scholars create as they study? These questions invite us to muddy the line that falsely separates theory from practice, the performer from the scholar, and performance from criticism.  This foundational course engages myriad modes of performance-making through a set of case studies across media (theater, music, dance, and visual arts). Designed for TDPS majors and nonmajors alike, students will engage key readings in performance theory, aesthetics, and the social worlds shaped by performance, while also learning to bridge their analysis to their own burgeoning artistic practices.

courses.title: Directed Research
courses.description: Empirical research projects or literature review. A student must be sponsored by a faculty member, who sets the requirements and supervises the student's progress. To register, the student must download a tutorial form from http://psychology.yale.edu/undergraduate/undergraduate-major-forms, complete it with the adviser, and submit it to the director of undergraduate studies by the deadline listed on the form. The normal minimum requirement is a written report of the completed research or literature review, but individual faculty members may set alternative equivalent requirements. May be elected for one or two terms.
courses.requirements: May not be used for the Psychology senior essay requirement.

courses.title: Research Topics
courses.description: Empirical research project or literature review. A student must be sponsored by a faculty member, who sets the requirements and supervises the student's progress. To register, the student must download a tutorial form from http://psychology.yale.edu/undergraduate/undergraduate-major-forms, complete it with the adviser, and submit it to the director of undergraduate studies by the date indicated on the form. The normal minimum requirement is a written report of the completed research or literature review, but individual faculty members may set alternative equivalent requirements. May be elected for one or two terms.
courses.requirements: May not be used for the Psychology senior essay requirement.

courses.title: Senior Essay
courses.description: Independent senior research project (either empirical research or literature review), conducted under the guidance of a faculty adviser who sets the requirements and supervises the research. To register, the student must download a tutorial form from http://psychology.yale.edu/undergraduate/undergraduate-major-forms, complete it with the adviser, and submit it by the deadline indicated on the form. The normal minimum requirement is a written report of the completed research or literature review, but individual faculty members may set alternative equivalent requirements. A paper of 5,000 words or more meets the writing needed for the senior requirement. To be considered for Distinction in the Major, the paper should be submitted at least one week before the last day of classes and will be graded by the adviser and a second reader assigned by the DUS.

courses.title: Classics of the Islamic World
courses.description: Islamic civilization has produced numerous works that would make it onto almost anyone’s list of wondrous books. In this course, we read a selection of (or from) those books and study the literary and intellectual cultures that produced them in an attempt to deepen and nuance our understanding of Islamic civilization. Readings include the Qur’an, classical Arabic poetry, the Shahnameh, Leyli ve Mejnun, the Conference of the Birds, the Hang Tuah Epic, and much else besides. All readings in translation.
courses.requirements: Previously offered as Classics: The Arabic-Islamic World.

courses.title: African Diaspora in the Americas
courses.description: In much of the world, Black people share a history of dispossession, oppression, and regeneration. This course explores how these diverse groups of Africans and their descendants survived spiritual catastrophe by creating new cultures, making common cause, and struggling together for liberation from slavery in the Americas. This broad survey highlights the politics of spiritual, communal, and political survival, showing how Africans and their descendants forged peoplehood in the crucible of human bondage. We consider the importance of speech, movement, music, image, letters, and religion in the making of the African diaspora by examining how these forms of expressive practice developed distinctly in different places from within a common process of displacement, suffering, struggle, and regeneration. The intricacies of Atlantic creole speech, the movement arts of Brazil, the music of Jamaica, the visual arts of Haiti, Cuba, and the antebellum United States, and the emerging literature of Black America will offer our primary examples of this process.

courses.title: A Twentieth-Century History of Migrant Imprisonment in the U.S.
courses.description: Like the nation’s prison system, today’s U.S. immigration detention apparatus is the largest of its kind in the world. By predominantly detaining migrants of color, it functions as a highly racialized carceral structure that excludes, removes, and punishes non–U.S. citizens. This seminar traces the historical relationship between migrants and the U.S. carceral state from the early twentieth century to the present. It examines how such an expansive system of migrant imprisonment and policing evolved and how struggles for freedom challenged carceral power. Key questions include: What is migrant incarceration? Who are the people who have been historically confined in migrant jails? What are the archival challenges of studying these histories? How have U.S. authorities revised immigration, asylum, and foreign policy to create a highly racialized immigration detention system? What is the transnational scope of the U.S. migrant carceral regime? How have immigration prisons become sites of racialization, politicization, and insurgence? In what historical context have migrants, local communities, activists, foreign governments, and U.S. policymakers contested—or consented to—the mass incarceration of non-U.S. citizens? How are the prison system and the immigration detention apparatus intertwined? Drawing on seminar discussions and themes, students will produce an original research paper.

courses.title: Antisemitism in Modern European History since 1900
courses.description: This course introduces students to the history of the term antisemitism as well as historical debates about its manifestations.  It focuses on Europe from the end of the nineteenth century, tracing the emergence of antisemitism in its modern form through interwar fascism and to the present, emphasizing discussions about whether a "new" antisemitism has emerged and focusing on efforts to restrain its manifestations by defining it broadly to include criticism of Israel.  We cover the central historical moments in the history of antisemitism in Europe, including the Dreyfus Affair, pogroms in the Pale of Settlement, Nazi Jew-hatred, and the twinning of antisemitism and anticommunism in the specter of the Jewish communist, dubbed "Judeo-Bolshevism." The last few weeks of the course are devoted to the rise of Islamophobia in Europe and its relationship to antisemitism, as well as current discussions of antisemitism’s resurgence.

courses.title: Dissidence and Control in Early Modern Spain and its Empire
courses.description: Aspects of Spanish culture and society in the Golden Age (c. 1550–1650) that demonstrate discontent, dissidence, and suggestions for reform. Emphasis on the intersection of historical and literary sources and the dynamic between popular and elite cultures.

courses.title: Literature of Suspense
courses.description: Exploration of suspense as a significant narrative mode and a historically conditioned feeling. Readings trace an arc from the rise of suspense in sentimental and Gothic fiction in the eighteenth century, through its preeminence in the nineteenth-century novel, to its consolidation as a marketable genre in the twentieth century. With brief supplemental readings in the philosophy of aesthetics and narrative theory.
courses.requirements: Enrollment limited to first-year students.

courses.title: China from Present to Past
courses.description: Underlying causes of current issues facing China traced back to their origins in the premodern period. Topics include economic development, corruption, environmental crises, gender, and Pacific island disputes. Selected primary-source readings in English, images, videos, and Web resources. Preference given to first years and sophomores.

courses.title: Brazil and the Afro-Atlantic World: Slavery, Emancipation, and Diaspora
courses.description: The present seminar reviews the history and historiography of Brazil as the largest and longest-lived slave regime in the Americas and a post-emancipated society that hid structural racism under ideologies of "racial democracy" within an Atlantic perspective connected to Africa. The course examines the cultural, social, and economic aspects of slavery, transatlantic slave trade, racialized violence, and racial inequality in Brazil from its origins in the sixteenth century, passing through the abolition of 1888 and finishing with the rise of Brazilian Black power movement in dialogue with African countries.

courses.title: Fundamentals of Neuroimaging
courses.description: The neuroenergetic and neurochemical basis of several dominant neuroimaging methods, including fMRI. Technical aspects of different methods, interpretation of results, and controversies or challenges regarding the application of fMRI and related methods in medicine.

courses.title: Introduction to the History of Antisemitism
courses.description: This course traces the development of animosity toward Jews and Judaism in different time periods and by diverse cultures, beginning in classical antiquity and continuing until the present. Through close examination of primary documents and the analysis of a variety of secondary sources, students build their understanding of the long history of this animosity, which we commonly refer to as "antisemitism." There is also an ongoing discussion of the difficulty of assigning a simple definition to a phenomenon that has been referred to as "the longest hatred."
courses.classnotes: Instructor: Linda Maizels
courses.requirements: This course offers an overview to an important topic and does not require or expect any specialized knowledge. All interested students are welcome.

courses.title: Water and Society: Culture, Life, and Values
courses.description: Water has become an urgent theme not just in current anthropology, but in development studies and environmental studies more generally. Beyond questions of scarcity and sustainability, water allows human life to flourish, and without water, there would be no civilization. Yet water is not equitably distributed across time or space, leading to contestation and conflict around water. Against such a background of strife, this course examines how human beings have related to water, to other life forms, and to each other through the control of water, in different historical moments and different parts of the world. The seminar is organized around four porous thematic clusters: (i) "urban water", to do with cities and urban industrial life; (ii) "agrarian water", to do with rivers, irrigation systems, and agrarian life; (iii) "rural water", to do with coasts, lakes, dams and rural life; and (iv) and "living water", to do with social, cultural and political values, and human and more-than-human life. This seminar introduces students to the everyday values of water, as well as the everyday politics of water, including the production of water and its attendant politics at the level of the nation-state as well as the city municipality while also being attentive to the moral ecologies of water. By studying water in different ways through the lens of culture, environment, social justice, and spirituality or faith, students develop a nuanced understanding of development, urbanization, environmental justice, and climate change.

courses.title: Advanced Software Engineering
courses.description: This course builds on CPSC 439 Software Engineering with a focus on a) building systems that scale well, and b) the technical infrastructure and approaches that would guide or inform entrepreneurship/business decisions. During the whole semester, teams work on a term-length software project of students' design, most often a continuation of the project they worked on during CPSC 4390 or CPSC 5390.
courses.requirements: After CPSC 4390 or similar. Students will have to have a working product they built during CPSC 4390 or similar course, to further develop during this course.

courses.title: Advanced Software Engineering
courses.description: This course builds on CPSC 439 Software Engineering with a focus on a) building systems that scale well, and b) the technical infrastructure and approaches that would guide or inform entrepreneurship/business decisions. During the whole semester, teams work on a term-length software project of students' design, most often a continuation of the project they worked on during CPSC 4390 or CPSC 5390.
courses.requirements: After CPSC 4390 or similar. Students will have to have a working product they built during CPSC 4390 or similar course, to further develop during this course.

courses.title: Colonialism and Psychology
courses.description: This seminar is a thematic exploration of colonialism as a historical, cultural, and, above all psychological experience. We explore topics such as the relation between Self and Other (Colonizer and Colonized) in the colonial encounter; the psychoanalysis of race and racism; violence and decolonization; psychopolitics; gender, language, and the intimacy of the colonial encounter; and the psychic life of the postcolony. We follow the itineraries of the renowned Martinican psychiatrist and philosopher Frantz Fanon (1925–1961) from the Antilles to metropolitan France, to colonial Algeria. We shall begin in the colony–‘Albert Camus’s Algeria’–and end in postcolonial Paris. We mobilize a diverse array of primary and secondary sources, novels, and films in our exploration, traversing Europe, the Antilles, and North Africa, with a primary emphasis on French colonialism in Algeria and its aftermath in the postcolony.

courses.title: Biomedical Natural Language Processing: Methods and Applications
courses.description: This course examines current natural language processing (NLP) methods and their applications in the biomedical domain. It provides a systematic introduction to basic knowledge on NLP and AI (e.g., linguistics, machine learning, and deep learning algorithms), advanced NLP tasks (e.g., information extraction, information retrieval, question answering), and corresponding approaches including the recent large language models (LLMs) and hands-on experience in developing biomedical NLP systems for different applications, ranging from biomedical literature mining to clinical decision support. Assessment in this course consists of technical exercises, exams, and projects, to demonstrate the applicability of skills learned during the course.

courses.title: Distributed Artificial Intelligence on Biomedical Data
courses.description: This course covers the basic concepts of artificial intelligence (AI), distributed ledger, and distributed AI with applications on biomedical data. We plan to cover AI pipeline, blockchain and smart contracts, and blockchain-based federated learning methods. By the end of this course, students should be able to: (1) select and use AI, distributed ledger, and distributed AI methods appropriate for a given clinical research content; (2) understand and apply AI, distributed ledger, and distributed AI approaches in the context of biomedical problems in research settings; (3) adapt, and validate AI, distributed ledger and distributed AI approaches to a specific biomedical problem; and (4) communicate audience-appropriate biomedical informatics content for AI, distributed ledger and distributed AI.

courses.title: Bioinformatics Applications in Biomedicine
courses.description: This advanced graduate course prepares students to analyze real-world biomedical data at scale across omics data and electronic health record (EHR) data. Emphasizing reproducible workflows, statistical rigor, and clinical translation, students work directly with large-scale omics datasets and biobank resources, including the All of Us Research Program. Through coding-intensive assignments, students develop Linux-based pipelines, Slurm-driven HPC workflows, cloud-native analyses, and EHR-based cohort construction for translational investigations. Student-led journal presentations strengthen algorithmic understanding, reproducibility, and translational thinking. Designed to complement theory-driven coursework, the course focuses on practical execution—equipping students to build scalable pipelines, generate biologically and clinically meaningful insights, and communicate methods with professional technical clarity.
courses.requirements: Proficiency in Python and R for data analysis.

courses.title: Computational Proteomics and Protein Modeling
courses.description: This course explores advanced computational proteomics and protein modeling approaches. Students gain hands-on experience analyzing bulk, single-cell, and imaging-based proteomics data. The course also covers cutting-edge machine learning and deep learning techniques, including transformer models, graph neural networks, and generative models, for protein-related tasks such as structure and function prediction and protein optimization. Special attention is given to applications in immunology. This course is ideal for students interested in computational biology, AI-driven structural biology, and computational immunology.
courses.requirements: Prerequisites: mathematics and statistics (linear algebra; calculus [for optimization]; probability/statistics), Python for data analysis (NumPy, Pandas, plotting, Jupyter; basic Git/conda), machine learning basics (regression/classification, model evaluation, intro to deep learning [PyTorch]). Recommended: basic biology (proteins [sequence/structure], high-level proteomics), advanced machine learning (transformers, GNNs, generative models, command-line tools).

courses.title: Foundations of Real World Data Science: Electronic Health Records
courses.description:
The course covers scientific principles, best practices, and limitations of using observational data from administrative records, including hypothesis generation, feasibility assessments, and causal inference. Students learn pragmatic skills required to prepare analytic data from large, complex transactional databases. We cover methods for data quality characterization and profiling for study planning. Coursework includes application of methods for creation and validation of computable phenotypes, electronic clinical quality measures, and derived analytic variables. Skills include preparation of real-world data for visualization and reporting in business intelligence tools commonly used in population health and health administration. Students reproduce results from published literature using existing databases for predictive modeling, public health, and outcomes research. Completion of this course positions students for externships in healthcare analytics and health data science.

BIS 638, Clinical Database Management Systems and Ontologies (or equivalent); proficiency in SQL and Python, or R; HIPAA and HSR training; YNHHS Research Basic Access; COS550 or equivalent; execution of DUAs for public and proprietary databases; demonstrated use of YU-YNHHS data science platform.
courses.requirements: Prerequisites: Course must be approved by the instructor

courses.title: Design and Evaluation of Biomedical and Health Informatics Solutions to Advance Health Equity
courses.description: This course focuses on the design and evaluation of biomedical and health informatics systems through a health equity lens while introducing core principles of research design. Through case studies, students learn foundational approaches to designing studies, measurement, and evaluation. Students apply research methods and evaluation frameworks to assess informatics systems. This course emphasizes practical skills for building and assessing informatics systems that promote health equity. Students examine how informatics systems can be intentionally designed to promote equitable processes and outcomes in clinical care, translational research, and public health settings. Through integrating interdisciplinary perspectives, this course prepares students to advance health equity through biomedical and health informatics research and practice.

courses.title: AI for Predictive Genomics: From Sequence to Disease
courses.description: This course examines the frontiers of computational genomics in the era of artificial intelligence, focusing on how modern AI/ML models are reshaping our ability to map sequence to regulation to cell state to disease. Rather than a broad survey, the course is organized around core problem classes—including biological sequence modeling, single-cell and spatial data integration, variant-to-function mapping, gene regulatory networks, perturbation modeling, and disease gene discovery. The course emphasizes a unifying view of genomics as a predictive problem linking DNA sequence to cellular and disease phenotypes through AI-driven models. Students will critically analyze state-of-the-art methods (e.g., foundation models, deep generative models, and large language models) and learn how they are used to solve real biological problems. Emphasis is placed on connecting methodological advances to biological questions, understanding model assumptions and limitations, and identifying open challenges. Through literature presentations and a project-driven format, students will design, implement, and evaluate AI/ML approaches on real genomics problems. The course also features invited lectures from researchers developing influential methods, providing direct exposure to ongoing work at the cutting edge.
courses.requirements: This is an advanced course in computational biology and does not provide a comprehensive introduction to basic concepts or methodologies. Students are expected to have completed entry-level coursework in probability and statistics, artificial intelligence (AI) or machine learning (ML), and genetics or genomics. Students should also be comfortable programming in Python or a similar language, as the final project involves implementing AI/ML methods to address real-world problems in computational genomics. Please contact the instructor if you have any questions regarding these prerequisites.

courses.title: Research Paper in Computational Biology and Biomedical Informatics (Part 2)
courses.description: This two-semester single credit pass/fail course must be completed as part of the terminal M.S. degree program in computational biology and biomedical informatics (CB&B). Students work with a faculty supervisor in designing their project and writing their research paper. The syllabus details the intended scope and process for writing the research paper. In the broadest terms, the research paper must be of publishable quality and defensible in a public scientific forum. The student’s research supervisor is responsible for managing the intended product. The preferred format of the research paper for students is one that is in the style and length of a publishable, peer-reviewed paper, templated based on the journal submission.
courses.requirements: Prerequisite: second-year enrollment in program.

courses.title: Intermediate Microeconomics
courses.description: The theory of resource allocation and its applications. Topics include the theory of choice, consumer and firm behavior, production, price determination in different market structures, welfare, and market failure.
courses.requirements: After introductory microeconomics and completion of Math 1120 or higher. Elementary techniques from multivariate calculus are introduced and applied, but prior knowledge is not assumed. May not be taken after ECON 2125.

courses.title: Observation
courses.description: What happens when, as visual artists, we narrow the gap between observing a subject and describing it? "Working from observation" is a phrase commonly used in art education, particularly in painting and drawing, yet is largely unexamined due to its rudimentary status in art school, associations with amateurism, and preliminary application in art practices throughout history. This seminar invites us to consider anew the creative and intellectual possibilities of observation through contemporary concerns, such as attention, reality, environment, objectivity/subjectivity, time, witness, and perception. Class periods and assignments will include a combination of hands-on learning, lectures, discussion, reading, and writing. Students will be invited to respond to experiential prompts in the media of their own choosing. Expert visitors in fields beyond and within the visual arts will deepen our understanding of how the body relates to the phenomenal and physical world. Readings and discussions will connect our discoveries to existing scholarship and research.
courses.requirements: Open to all MFA students.

courses.title: Curating the Global Contemporary: Enwezor and Legacies
courses.description: This course will survey the curatorial and scholarly work of renowned curator and thinker, Okwui Enwezor (1963—2019). Having curated some of the most important exhibitions in the last four decades, including the Johannesburg Biennial, the Venice Biennale, Archive Fever, and Documenta, to name a few, Enwezor's work has provided a much-needed framework for decentering conventional and Eurocentric canons that have continued to benefit the few (at the expense of others). Situated in what he once called a "change-agenda," Enwezor's editorial, theoretical, and curatorial work engages with the core principles of representation and how these intersect with the construction and dissemination of culture. As he put it, "representation becomes not merely the name for a manner of practice, but, quite literally, the name for a political awareness of identity within the field of representation. In the context of decolonized representation, innovation is about the coming to being of new relations to cultures and histories, to rationalizations and transformations, to transculturation and assimilation, and new practices and processes, as well as the ways in which artists are seen to be bound to their national and cultural traditions."  The seminar will engage such questions as: what can an exhibition as a vessel be? What is the lexicon of untranslatables that shapes a multipolar world? How can curatorial practice attune to the "lower frequencies" of unseen, opaque, and fugitive worlds-in-common? Amidst necropolitical catastrophe, what wagers of the in-common are we nonetheless able to stake?

courses.title: Prospectus Writing Workshop
courses.description: A non-credit workshop for third-year Ph.D. students in the Political Science department, in which they develop, revise, and present their prospectus.

courses.title: Directed Reading with Senior Fellow
courses.description: Directed reading or individual project option is designed for qualified students who wish to investigate an area not covered in regular graduate-level courses. The student must be supervised by a senior fellow, who sets the requirements and meets regularly with the student. Usually limited to one per semester, this option may involve reading the literature on a topic, attending a lecture or seminar series, and writing a substantial research paper. It is the student’s responsibility to make all the arrangements before the semester begins.

courses.title: Directed Reading
courses.description: Directed reading or individual project option is designed for qualified students who wish to investigate an area not covered in regular graduate-level courses. The student must be supervised by a faculty member, who sets the requirements and meets regularly with the student. Usually limited to one per semester, this option may involve reading the literature on a topic, attending a lecture or seminar series, and writing a substantial research paper. It is the student’s responsibility to make all the arrangements before the semester begins.
courses.requirements: By arrangement with faculty.

courses.title: Global Affairs Thesis
courses.description: The thesis is an optional yearlong research project that is completed in the final academic year of the M.P.P. degree. It is intended for students who wish to make a major policy-oriented research project the culmination of the student’s educational experience in the program. M.P.P. theses involve independently performed research by the student under the supervision of a faculty adviser. Students work with faculty advisers in designing their project and in writing the thesis. Detailed guidelines for the thesis are outlined in the Jackson School of Global Affairs Bulletin.
courses.requirements: Prerequisite: GLBL 9990

courses.title: The First World War
courses.description: This class explores the causes and consequences of the First World War. In doing so, we emphasize the ways in which the story of the war, far from constituting a series of military battles, is a political, social, cultural, economic, and environmental history, focusing on the experience of the war for everyday soldiers and citizens. While the First World War started in Europe, we also delve into the experiences of places outside Europe. The readings and course materials are primary sources produced during the war period, as well as cultural artifacts that allow us to explore its memory.

courses.title: The Economics of Gender
courses.description: This seminar course is about the economics of gender and has a focus on labor and marriage markets. Students are given an overview of gender differences in these markets, as well as some potential reasons for those differences. The course also discusses policies that can affect the gender gaps.
courses.requirements: Prerequisites: ECON 121 or 125, and ECON 117, or equivalent.

courses.title: Broadway to Beyonce: Dance in American Popular Culture
courses.description: This lecture surveys the role of dance in American popular culture. Starting with the roots of American popular dance in the 18th and 19th centuries, the course focuses on the 20th and 21st, tracking the intersection of dance and music and the dissemination of both through stage, film, music videos, concerts, and the internet. The course pays special attention to how dance forms that originated in Black communities have spread through the wider culture, via Broadway shows, Hollywood films, television programs, and YouTube. The course draws its subject matter mostly from primary sources, mainly film and video, but also samples a wide variety of authors and perspectives.

courses.title: The Senior Essay
courses.description: All senior History majors should attend the mandatory senior essay meeting in early September at a time and location to be announced in the online Senior Essay Handbook. The senior essay is a required one- or two-term independent research project conducted under the guidance of a faculty adviser. As a significant work of primary-source research, it serves as the capstone project of the History major. Students writing the one-term senior essay enroll in HIST 497 (see description), not HIST 495 and 496. The two-term essay takes the form of a substantial article, not longer than 12,500 words (approximately forty to fifty double-spaced typewritten pages). This is a maximum limit; there is no minimum requirement. Length will vary according to the topic and the historical techniques employed. Students writing the two-term senior essay who expect to graduate in May enroll in HIST 495 during the fall term and complete their essays in HIST 496 in the spring term. December graduates enroll in HIST 495 in the spring term and complete their essays in HIST 496 during the following fall term; students planning to begin their essay in the spring term should notify the senior essay director by early December. Each student majoring in History must present a completed Statement of Intention, signed by a department member who has agreed to serve as adviser, to the History Department Undergraduate Registrar by the dates indicated in the Senior Essay Handbook. Blank statement forms are available from the History Undergraduate Registrar and in the Senior Essay handbook. Students enrolled in HIST 495 submit to the administrator in 237 HGS a two-to-three-page analysis of a single primary source, a draft bibliographic essay, and at least ten pages of the essay by the deadlines listed in the Senior Essay Handbook. Those who meet these requirements receive a temporary grade of SAT for the fall term, which will be changed to the grade received by the essay upon its completion. Failure to meet any requirement may result in the student’s being asked to withdraw from HIST 495. Students enrolled in HIST 496 must submit a completed essay to 211 HGS no later than 5 p.m. on the dates indicated in the Senior Essay Handbook. Essays submitted after 5 p.m. will be considered as having been turned in on the following day. If the essay is submitted late without an excuse from the student's residential college dean, the penalty is one letter grade for the first day and one-half letter grade for each of the next two days past the deadline. No essay that would otherwise pass will be failed because it is late, but late essays will not be considered for departmental or Yale College prizes. All senior departmental essays will be judged by members of the faculty other than the adviser. In order to graduate from Yale College, a student majoring in History must achieve a passing grade on the departmental essay.

courses.title: One-Term Senior Essay
courses.description: All senior History majors should attend the mandatory senior essay meeting in early September at a time and location to be announced in the online Senior Essay Handbook. The senior essay is a required one- or two-term independent research project conducted under the guidance of a faculty adviser. As a significant work of primary-source research, it serves as the capstone project of the History major. Seniors writing a two-term senior essay do not register for HIST 497; instead, they register for HIST 495 and HIST 496 (see description). History majors may choose to write a one-term independent senior essay in the first term of their senior year and register for HIST 497; however, students who choose the one-term senior essay option are not eligible for Distinction in the Major. The one-term essay must include a substantial research paper of no more than 6,250 words (approximately twenty-five pages) based on primary sources, along with a bibliographic essay and bibliography. Seniors enroll during the fall term of senior year; only History majors graduating in December may enroll during the spring term (or seventh term of enrollment). In rare circumstances, with the permission of the adviser and the Senior Essay Director, a student enrolled in HIST 497 during the fall term may withdraw from the course according to Yale College regulations on course withdrawal and enroll in the spring term. Each student enrolled in HIST 497 must present a completed Statement of Intention, signed by a department member who has agreed to serve as adviser, to the History Department Undergraduate Registrar by the dates indicated in the Senior Essay Handbook. Blank statement forms are available from the History Undergraduate Registrar and in the Senior Essay Handbook, available on the History department Web site. Additional details about the senior essay, including the submission deadlines are included in the Senior Essay Handbook. Essays submitted after 5 p.m. on the due date will be considered as having been turned in on the following day. If the essay is submitted late without an excuse from the student's residential college dean, the penalty is one letter grade for the first day and one-half letter grade for each of the next two days past the deadline. No essay that would otherwise pass will be failed because it is late. All senior departmental essays will be judged by members of the faculty other than the adviser. In order to graduate from Yale College, a student majoring in History must achieve a passing grade on the departmental essay. Permission of the departmental Senior Essay Director and of the student’s faculty adviser is required for enrollment.

courses.title: Methods and Logic in Interdisciplinary Research
courses.description: This full PEB class is intended to introduce students to integrated approaches to research. Each week, the first of two sessions is student-led, while the second session is led by faculty with complementary expertise and discusses papers that use different approaches to the same topic (for example, physical and biological or experiment and theory).

courses.title: Herpetology
courses.description: An examination of the origin and evolution of amphibians and reptiles with particular emphasis on global diversity, the fossil record, and the evolution of body plans. Discussion of classic and current literature provides a sense of the state of the art. Detailed hands-on study of external and internal anatomy heavily employs the collections of the Yale Peabody Museum.
courses.requirements: Prerequisites: BIOL 1010-1040, high-school AP-equivalent preparation, or permission of instructor. E-mail instructor for options if considering alongside EPS 3250.

courses.title: Advanced Dance Repertory
courses.description: A studio intensive that explores Alvin Ailey’s unique craft as a choreographer and master storyteller, with a focus on his lesser-known relationship to jazz and the music of Duke Ellington. Ailey created a company that both celebrated the African American experience and preserved and advanced the modern dance tradition. Students encounter these ideas through learning excerpts of Ailey’s master works. The course covers a full reconstruction of Mr. Ailey’s dance "Night Creature" (1975), with excerpts folded in from "The River" (1971/1980), both with music by Ellington, and his seminal work "Revelations" (1960), among other choreographies. A historical study of Ailey’s import complements this movement research, including special attention to the aesthetic and political reverberations of his technique and methods, and his influence on younger choreographers, in the work of Ron Brown and Jamar Roberts. The semester culminates in an invited studio showing.
courses.requirements: Prior dance training is required. Admission by audition.

courses.title: Anatomy and Movement
courses.description:
This course traces connections between the study of  human anatomy and dance practices of the late 20th century to the present. Over the past century, a group of pioneering practitioners sought to combine advances in human anatomical and neuromuscular science with the felt, practically applied knowledge of dance artists. Their research has spawned an array of new methods for training dance and theater artists, including ideokinesis, somatics, and body-mind centering. Immersing students in a studio-based, practical exploration, this course introduces students to key ideas and thinkers in the field of dance science.  Major topics include the study of functional and kinesthetic anatomy; the neuromuscular reeducation of alignment, posture and balance; the use of imagery as a motivator of movement; and the cultivation of enhanced mind-body awareness through physical practice. 

No prior experience in dance or theater necessary. This course is open to students of all physical abilities and backgrounds. The instructor will work with students with special needs or specific physical disabilities to adapt the movement exercises to meet their capabilities.
courses.requirements: Enrollment limited to first-year students.

courses.title: Introduction to International Relations
courses.description: Survey of key debates and concepts in international relations. Exploration of historical and contemporary issues using Western and non-Western cases and evidence. Topics include the rise of states; causes, conduct, and outcomes of wars; the emergence of new actors and forms of conflict; and evolution of global economy.

courses.title: Constitutional Law
courses.description: An introduction to the main themes of the American Constitution—popular sovereignty, separation of powers, federalism, and rights—and to basic techniques of constitutional interpretation. Special emphasis on the interplay of constitutional text, judicial doctrine, and constitutional decision making outside the judiciary.

courses.title: The Politics of Local Development
courses.description: Over the last several decades, countries across the Global South have undertaken a degree of decentralization—a downward shift in political and fiscal powers to local governments. Concurrently, international development agencies increasingly emphasize the importance of community participation in local interventions.
