courses.title: Advanced Topics in AI Security
courses.description: AI models undergoing internal cybersecurity evaluations at OpenAI bypassed containment controls, interacted with external web services, and compromised systems at Hugging Face. Anthropic accused Moonshot AI of covertly routing requests from users of its Kimi models to Claude and collecting Claude’s outputs and reasoning traces to train its own models. Shortly after, Anthropic reported incidents in which Claude models accessed third-party systems without authorization or submitted information to real websites, including submitting a false tip through a police department’s online form. All three of these incidents happened in the last few months, and they raise big questions about AI security: both the risks that AI systems create when given access to tools, and the ways these systems can themselves be attacked or compromised. This seminar introduces you to the large (and growing) field of AI security, which touches on both of these overarching sets of issues. We begin with some of the classic papers in machine learning security, from before the widespread deployment of generative AI, and steadily progress through some of today’s most pressing technical, safety, and governance questions. Topics include adversarial examples, data poisoning, privacy attacks, training-data extraction, model stealing and exfiltration, distillation attacks, prompt injection, and security risks involving autonomous agents. A central theme of the seminar is how deliberately breaking models and systems can help researchers understand their capabilities, limitations, and risks. But demonstrating an attack isn’t necessarily the same as establishing a meaningful real-world vulnerability. Throughout the course, we critically examine the threat models, assumptions, and empirical evidence underlying security research, as well as the effectiveness of proposed defenses. We also contextualize this research within broader discussions about AI safety and governance. By the end of the course, students are able to read and critically evaluate AI security papers, identify open research questions, and formulate their own research ideas. We also explore how AI security draws on and contributes to many different areas of research in computer science, including machine learning, computer security, privacy, and AI safety.
courses.requirements: Prerequisite: an introductory course in machine learning and/or statistics.

courses.title: Intensive Algorithms
courses.description: Mathematically sophisticated treatment of the design and analysis of algorithms and the theory of NP completeness. Algorithmic paradigms including greedy algorithms, divide and conquer, dynamic programming, network flow, approximation algorithms, and randomized algorithms. Problems drawn from the social sciences, Data Science, Computer Science, and engineering. For students with a flair for proofs and problem solving. Only one of CPSC 3650, CPSC 3660, or CPSC 3680 may be taken for credit.
courses.requirements: Prerequisites: MATH 2440 and CPSC 2230.

courses.title: Historical Perspectives on Science and Religion
courses.description: The engagement between science and religion from a historical standpoint and a multicultural perspective. The Islamic, Jewish, Buddhist, and Christian traditions; the roots of modern creationism; salvation expectations and the rise of modern science and technology.

courses.title: Greek Tragedy in Performance
courses.description: Greek tragedy is both a literary and a theatrical phenomenon. It emerged in the ancient city-state of Athens and peaked in the 5th century BCE. The distinct rules governing its poetic composition and theatrical execution were repeatedly renegotiated across cultures in the modern era – including in Greece. The course investigates the inherent tension of Greek tragedy as both "poem" and "performance script" through a parallel study of its texts (in English translation) and filmed stagings from around the world. Students develop a clear understanding of the subject matter of Greek tragedy, alongside its historical, artistic, and socio-political contexts and conventions in antiquity and in modern times. Through systematic exposure to and rigorous analysis of textual, directorial, design, and performance choices, they explore the theatrical possibilities of Greek tragedy in modern times and cultivate their own directorial and dramaturgical thinking.

courses.title: Close Analysis of Film
courses.description: Close study of a range of major films from a variety of periods and places. Apart from developing tools for the close analysis of film, we consider such topics as genre and mode; the role of sound; cinema as a structure of gazes; remakes and adaptations; approaches to realism; narration and resistance to narration; film in relation to other moving image media; and the relationship of close analysis to historical contextualization and interpretation more generally.
courses.requirements: Prerequisite: FILM 150.

courses.title: Landscape, Film, Architecture
courses.description: Movement through post-1945 landscapes and cityscapes as a key to understanding them. The use of cameras and other visual-verbal means as a way to expand historical, aesthetic, and sociological inquiries into how these places are inhabited and experienced. Exploration of both real and imaginary spaces in works by filmmakers (Wenders, Herzog, Ottinger, Geyrhalter, Seidl, Ade, Grisebach), architects and sculptors (e.g. Rudofsky, Neutra, Abraham, Hollein, Pichler, Smithson, Wurm, Kienast), photographers (Sander, B. and H. Becher, Gursky, Höfer), and writers (Bachmann, Handke, Bernhard, Jelinek). Additional readings by Certeau, Freytag, J.B. Jackson, L. Burckhardt.

courses.title: Current Topics in Chemical Biology
courses.description: This module examines current research in chemical biology through close, critical reading of the primary literature. Papers are drawn from active areas of the field and evaluated with the rigor of a referee: students learn to identify a paper's central claim, assess whether the experimental logic supports it, judge the adequacy of controls, and define the limits of what the data actually establish. The instructor leads the opening meetings by modeling a full referee-style evaluation of an assigned paper. Students lead the remaining sessions, each presenting a written review of an assigned article to open class discussion. Assessment is by in-class examination, combining discussion of topics covered during the term with the guided evaluation of a previously unseen excerpt from the primary literature.
courses.classnotes: This course is meeting first half of term
courses.requirements: Prerequisite: CHEM 4190/5190.

courses.title: Mass Spectrometry for Chemical Biology: Principles and Applications
courses.description: This module covers the principles and practice of modern mass spectrometry as applied to problems in chemical biology. Topics include ionization methods, the operating principles and performance characteristics of common mass analyzers, tandem mass spectrometry and gas-phase fragmentation chemistry, and strategies for quantitation. Later sessions address the analysis of post-translational modifications, with emphasis on glycosylation and the specific analytical challenges it presents. Students learn to interpret spectra, match instrumentation and acquisition strategy to a given biological question, and critically assess mass spectrometry data reported in the chemical biology literature.
courses.classnotes: Course meets in the Second Half of Term (0.5 credit)
courses.requirements: Prerequisite: CHEM 4190/5190.

courses.title: 3D Personalized Medicine Master’s Research Thesis
courses.description: Faculty-supervised individual projects with emphasis on research, laboratory, or theory. Students must define the scope of the proposed project with the faculty member who has agreed to act as supervisor and submit a thesis proposal for approval. Students have the option of working on 3D medical innovation projects with biomedical engineering companies, industry leaders of personalized medicine providing students with a year-long internship / "internal interview" with a biomedical technology company’s engineering team. These projects may involve the student developing novel software, hardware, manufacturing validations, medical devices, surgical instruments, or 3D printing modalities. The class meets weekly to review topics such as IRB protocols, ethics and HIPAA, biostatistics, research design, scientific writing, and presentation skills. This course is open only to graduate students enrolled in the M.S. in Personalized Medicine and Applied Engineering.

courses.title: Black Nature
courses.description: Drowned in the ocean during the trans-Atlantic slave trade, forced to cultivate the soil on plantations, or lynched from trees across the Jim Crow South, black Americans are entangled with nature in incredibly complex and precarious ways. In contrast to a largely white tradition of nature writing that assumes a superior position outside of Nature, this course undertakes a broad survey of African American writing about nature. Over the course of the semester, we read broadly across several genres of African American literature while also exploring recent scholarship around black environmentalisms and ecologies. In this way, we center the unique environmental perspectives of those, who, once considered no more than livestock, were the nature over which their white masters ruled. But perhaps who also, for this very reason, may be recognized as pioneering a sustainable human life in nature, rather than apart from it.

courses.title: German Science(-ish) Fictions
courses.description: Throughout modernity, science has relied on metaphors, narratives, and thought experiments, while literature and film have borrowed the language of experiment, evidence, and measurement. This course explores these collisions between science and fiction in German-language cultural production through works of literature, film, and philosophy. Readings include works by Leibniz, Goethe, E. T. A. Hoffmann, Paul Scheerbart, Rainer Maria Rilke, Franz Kafka, and Raphaela Edelbauer alongside films by Fritz Lang and Rainer Werner Fassbinder. Designed as both an advanced language course and a seminar in German-speaking literature and culture, this course will help students strengthen their reading, writing, speaking, listening, and analytical skills in German.
courses.requirements: Prerequisites: L4 German or the equivalent.

courses.title: Modern Liberty
courses.description: Debates about the meaning of freedom from the eighteenth, nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Authors to be studied include Smith, Montesquieu, Constant, Tocqueville, Mill, Marx and Schmitt. Major themes include the promise and pitfalls of commercial society, the relation between religion and freedom, the understanding of ourselves as historical beings, the question of progress, political representation, constitutionalism, democracy and individuality.
courses.requirements: Prerequisite: One course in political theory, intellectual history or philosophy.

courses.title: Gender, Sex, and Science in the Modern United States
courses.description: In January 2025, Donald Trump signed an executive order that mandated that there are only "two sexes, male and female." In this seminar, we use the methods of historical inquiry to examine this biological premise. This seminar explores how scientific and medical ideas––and contentious debates––about sex, gender, and sexuality have impacted politics and social life in the modern United States. We track how new categories like "biological sex," "gender identity," and "sexual identity" were developed in the human and medical sciences and used to regulate human identity, childhood, marital and family life, and racial divides from the late nineteenth century through the present. Topics include the rise of sexology, psychoanalysis, trans medicine, conversion therapy, and place of science and medicine in the history of queer and trans politics. Our course ends by contextualizing the rise of current-day debates about trans medicine, "gender ideology," and the continued significance of science and medicine for arbitrating the bounds of human identity today.

courses.title: School Choice, Policy, and Segregation
courses.description: Do parents know best (as the US Department of Education repeatedly announces)? School choice has been an ascending education policy in the United States and globally over the last quarter century. We examine the theoretical underpinnings of school choice and its history in the United States and globally. We also investigate how families choose schools for their children, and whether the choices themselves- whether charter schools, magnet schools, vouchers, private schools, and homeschooling advance or limit access to equitable education. The course examines several US and global school choice case studies, including a hands-on investigation of school choice in New Haven.
courses.requirements: Prerequisites: EDST 1110: Foundations of Education Studies (recommended)

courses.title: American Political Economy: Institutions, Interests, and Inequalities
courses.description: This course examines the American political economy―the ways in which the U.S.' distinctive political institutions mediate the relationship between markets and governance and produce fundamental social outcomes. Topics include the power of economic interests, rise of the knowledge economy, and territorial distribution of economic and political advantage in America's federated system of governance.
courses.requirements: This course requires sufficient prior coursework in political science to grasp high-level concepts and research.

courses.title: Aristotle and Kant
courses.description: An intensive study of Aristotelian ethics, Kantian morality, and the political visions constructed on these foundations. Texts include Aristotle’s Nicomachean Ethics and Politics; Kant’s Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals and various political essays; and selections from contemporary theorists such as Danielle Allen, Martha Nussbaum, John Rawls, and Jürgen Habermas. In the company of Aristotle, Kant, and theorists inspired by them, we examine fundamental questions and contemporary debates.

courses.title: The Space Domain and Global Security
courses.description: The outer space domain is increasingly important to global security and prosperity. Space capabilities enable unprecedented economic opportunities across multiple fields of endeavor, ranging from environment and agriculture to transportation, science, and banking.  At the same time, space has become essential to national defense: it underpins the ability of advanced militaries to navigate and track forces, to maintain robust communications, to detect missile launches, and to ensure effective command and control.  Yet the evolution in uses of space, and advances in space technology, create novel risks, vulnerabilities, and threats. This course aims to equip students with an understanding of the dynamic, rapidly evolving domain of outer space.  After analyzing some of the unique technical and legal features of the space domain, the class explores the strategic significance of space to American national security interests, particularly as space becomes more competitive among nations. The course also focuses on the rise of the commercial space industry, the growing number of space activities undertaken by corporations, and the role of public-private partnerships in ensuring the resilience of national space assets and the global space economy. In collaboration with the U.S. Air Force Academy, students also participate in an intensive space conflict tabletop exercise, assuming the roles of key stakeholders in an engaging simulation.
courses.requirements: There are no formal prerequisites for this course.  However, for those seeking admission—especially undergraduates—must submit a statement of interest to the instructors for consideration—prior coursework or work experience in global affairs, law, computer science, physics, astrophysics, and/or astronomy, is helpful.  Students will be admitted to the course from a diverse array of backgrounds.

courses.title: Human Evolution
courses.description: The main objective of this course is for students to learn how evidence and theory intersect with some of the peculiarities of history to form the modern discipline of paleoanthropology. It deals with scientific questions of human origins and evolution, and what we think we know of our own ancestry over the past 6 million years. We cover key tools such as evolutionary theory, paleontology, archaeology, paleoenvironmental reconstruction, phylogenetic analysis, genetics, and functional morphology. Using these tools, we critically examine what key debates have taken place over the last century of exploration and discovery in human evolutionary research, learning how unconventional thinking and spectacular discoveries have shaped current knowledge of our origins. Students learn what a surprising amount of information scientists can discern from fragmentary fossils, and are brought up to date with the most current discoveries and debates in human evolution. Students also see how human origins are conveyed to a broader audience, and how misunderstandings about how it happened can propagate and be misused.
courses.requirements: Knowledge of introductory biological anthropology or biology are helpful.

courses.title: Rome after Rome
courses.description: How often do you think about the Roman Empire? And why do some people ruminate about it so much? This first-year seminar looks at Rome as a conceptual resource, explored across 5 thematic units: history and politics, film, literature, popular media, and material culture. Designed as an introduction to Rome and its reception, the course studies how Rome’s legacy was constructed, contested, and mobilized after antiquity. What are the uses of Rome after Rome? Which Rome are we talking about? And how does an ancient civilization inform modern culture? Participants will learn to critically engage with textual and visual material, improve written and oral communication, and use primary and secondary sources to make succinct, well-supported arguments.
courses.requirements: Enrollment limited to first-year students.

courses.title: Conceptualizing the Citizen
courses.description: Citizenship is a slippery target in the ancient Greek world. It had various and changing legal definitions throughout time and space. Citizenship conveyed status and promised privileges; it was jealously guarded and occasionally granted. What can be said for certain is that the meaning of "citizen" was always open to redefinition and contestation. In this course, students survey a variety of Greek prose authors in the original language who grappled with the meaning of citizenship and its ideological underpinning. This course is a bridge course designed to help students transition from intermediate (L4) to advanced (L5) Greek.
courses.requirements: Prerequisite: L4 Ancient Greek

courses.title: Livy's Rome
courses.description: Close reading of selections from Livy's Ab Urbe Condita, including Books V and XXI in Latin and additional books in English translation. The nature of representation; Augustan elements in Livy's work; themes and plots of Livian history; Livy and other Roman historians; comparison of ancient historiography and contemporary historical writing. This course is a "bridge" course, which serves as a transition from intermediate (L4) to advanced (L5) Latin.
courses.requirements: Prerequisite: LATN 2004 or the equivalent. For questions about language placement, contact James Patterson, the Language Program Director in Classics.

courses.title: Myth, Land, and Power: Reading Ancient Greece and Rome
courses.description: This first-year seminar is about how the stories we tell shape us, our values, and the culture(s) we live in through the lens of Greek and Roman mythology. Land can be many things depending on our worldview: ancestor and relative, home, country vs. city, nature vs. cultivated place, unknown opportunity, resource, or property. Students in this class gain a deeper understanding of the land stories they inherit, what they wish to continue to carry forward, and what they may need to leave behind to live in accordance with their values. Together we think concretely about Greek and Roman myth and the resonances and dissonances with the wide range of land stories that shape our world. Key Course Questions include: 1a. How could these myths affect Greeks’ and Romans’ relationship to and with land? 1b. What are our relationships to land? 2a. What values are promoted in Greek and Roman myths about land? 2b. How do these stories reflect and enact cultural values? 3a. How is land characterized? 3b. Is land gendered? 4a. What is the role of violence in shaping these characters’ interactions with each other and with land? 4b. How is this violence framed in the narrative?
courses.requirements: Enrollment limited to first-year students.

courses.title: The Origins, Criticisms, and Legacy of the Athenian Democracy
courses.description: Ancient Athens was the birthplace of democracy — a radical experiment in popular rule that flourished, evolved, and collapsed within two centuries. But the democratic experiment never really ended. This course traces how the ancient Athenian democracy was built, how it functioned, its institutions, its leaders, its limitations, and its skeptics. We also attend to the afterlife of Athenian popular rule: the centuries of criticism, contestation, and reinvention through which the Athenian government became a (real or imaginary) template for many constitutions people live under today.

courses.title: Quintus of Smyrna
courses.description: A survey of the Posthomerica, the third century CE "sequel" to the Iliad composed by the poet known as Quintus of Smyrna. The seminar studies this Imperial epic poem under two angles: (i) its literary identity and the way(s) in which it positions itself as "late"; and (ii) its use of epic diction as a deliberate continuation of the development of Homer as language.

courses.title: Roman Satire
courses.description: The course focuses on Roman satirists, from Lucilius to Juvenal, looking at satire as a whole (both formal verse satire and polymetric "Menippean" satire, as well as "satiric" works that are not counted as satire per se, e.g., Petronius, Martial). Representative samples of all the major satirists are read alongside an array of recent scholarly studies. The late antique, medieval, early modern, and later receptions of Roman satire are folded into seminar throughout the semester and given special attention at the end.

courses.title: Evolution of Primate Intelligence
courses.description: Discussion of the extent and evolutionary origins of cognitive abilities in primates (prosimians, monkeys, apes, and humans). Topics include the role of ecological and social factors as evolutionary forces; "ape language" studies; and whether any nonhuman primates possess a "theory of mind."

courses.title: The Holocaust on the Eastern Front: History and Memory
courses.description: By the time Nazi Germany invaded the Soviet Union in June 1941, the USSR had become home to the world’s largest Jewish population—more than five million people. Roughly half would perish in the Holocaust. With Operation Barbarossa, the systematic mass murder of European Jews entered a new and decisive phase. Despite a substantial and growing body of scholarship, the Holocaust on the Eastern Front remains one of its less thoroughly explored dimensions. This seminar examines the Holocaust across the territories of the former Soviet Union, focusing on the distinctive forms it assumed in Ukraine, Belarus, Russia, Latvia, Lithuania, and Moldova. We study not only how Jews were murdered, but who they were, how they sought to survive, how they resisted, and how they fought Nazi Germany in the Red Army and partisan units. Particular attention is paid to local collaboration in identifying, robbing, guarding, deporting, and murdering Jews, as well as to postwar investigations and trials of collaborators. The seminar also explores Soviet and post-Soviet memory of the Holocaust and its place in contemporary debates over occupation, collaboration, national identity, and victimhood. Students engage with competing scholarly interpretations and work extensively with diverse primary sources.

courses.title: Nature, AI, and Performance
courses.description: Can sound convey information? This interdisciplinary course explores how new technologies, such as artificial intelligence together with environmental data mapping, can deepen our understanding of the physical world and how performance might further enhance that understanding. Indeed, before and after Aristotle, the movement and behavior of large animal groups, such as the flocking of birds, have long fascinated humanity. Students will engage in hands-on experiments that translate natural phenomena—like avian murmuration or shifting ecosystems—into dynamic performative expressions, including music, movement, and visual installations. CCAM technologies in the Leeds Studio, including the motion capture system, multichannel sound system, and AI-driven data sonification and visualization software (developed with a Yale Planetary Solutions Seed Grant), allow course participants to collaborate across disciplines and interpret complex environmental processes in creative ways. Through this semester-long investigation of the physical world to the digital and back to the physical, students will develop new modes of storytelling that blend the arts and sciences to communicate the complexities of our planet.

courses.title: Growth and Environmentalism
courses.description: Orienting public policy around economic growth was one of the defining features of 20th century politics. Whatever their political stripe—capitalist, socialist or communist—national governments focused on developing policies that would increase productivity, strengthen the country’s economic base, and advance material well-being. Yet many see today that this model of development is at risk of breaking down. Some argue that climate change and other environmental problems cannot be solved through scientific or technological breakthroughs alone, but rather through structural changes in the organization of economic and social life. This course looks at these critiques of growth, beginning with 20th century environmentalist critiques of industrial build-up, technological change and endless growth. The course surveys major ideas in mainstream economic growth theory, from Solow’s growth model and GDP to human capital theory and the environmental Kuznets curve. It contrasts these ideas with alternative approaches to economics that point to environmental ethics and stewardship, as well as human and ecological well-being, as starting points for economic theory, including E.F. Schumacher’s "Small is Beautiful," sustainable development, ecological economics, "nowtopia," and degrowth. We ask throughout what economic ideas might lead to more sustainable and equitable approaches to environmental policy in the 21st century.

courses.title: Environmental Politics
courses.description: Climate change, coupled with relentless pressure on the earth’s resources, has intensified the need for policy responses at local, national, and global levels. Yet breakdowns in political leadership, public disenchantment, and popular backlash mean that we must also consider what it means to build a meaningful environmental politics in the 21st century: What issues speak to most Americans, what arguments might prove effective, what changes are needed in existing institutions? We address these questions by looking at the history, evolution, and dynamics of environmental politics in the United States, with a focus on events since the 1960s. The course is designed with the following aims: learn about major stages in American environmental thought and their reflection in policy; gain an overview of key environmental writings, actors, institutions, processes, and events; explore important policy concepts (e.g., risk, regulation, sustainability, environmental justice); relate US environmental politics to developments in other countries and emerging global perspectives; and develop critical tools for environmental policy analysis. Through this work, students gain critical insight into what Americans historically valued about the environment and how agreement might again be forged on the purposes of environmental politics.

courses.title: King of the Jews: Royal Power and Jewish Political Culture, Ancient to Modern
courses.description: This seminar returns to one of history’s most consequential institutions – kingship – asking what millennia of Jewish engagement with royal power can teach us about sovereignty, representation, and dependency. Judaism’s relationship to kingship is profoundly ambivalent. The same tradition that produced enduring royal theologies also harbors a deep and systematic suspicion of monarchs. This tension is not a contradiction to be resolved but a generative force that has shaped Jewish political culture from antiquity to the present. The course traces this double stance from the Hebrew Bible through encounters with Near Eastern, Hellenistic, and Roman rulers; Jewish negotiations with Christian and Muslim medieval sovereigns; the age of absolutism; and the republican transformations of the nineteenth century. It concludes by examining how these dynamics persist in modernity through Zionism, the establishment of a Jewish state, and the reemergence of antisemitic tropes about Jewish power.

courses.title: Constitutions Under Strain
courses.description: Can a constitution stop an elected autocrat? It is often said that today’s would-be autocrats rarely seize power by force; they win elections, erode institutions, and exploit constitutional forms to stay in power. This seminar explores the populist challenge to constitutionalism: from a comparative perspective, we study how constitutions operate as shields, targets, or weapons in processes of democratic backsliding and repair. The course has three parts. The first asks what a constitution is and why constitutional comparison is not a purely academic endeavor but something political actors do, as when El Salvador’s president defended abolishing term limits by citing other democracies. The second follows the authoritarian playbook and the efforts to counter it: how populist leaders win power and keep it, and whether courts, watchdogs, and international bodies can stop them, with cases ranging from the United States to India. The third asks what comes after constitutional erosion: whether repair is possible, and whether some hallmark constitutional institutions are actually part of the problem, obstructing democracy and fueling populism. For students interested in law and politics, the seminar offers an accessible introduction to where the two meet most visibly. No prior experience required. Guests will join some sessions.

courses.title: Hip Hop Music and Culture
courses.description: The evolution of hip hop music and culture from the 1970s through the 1990s, including graffiti art, b-boying (break dancing), DJ-ing, and MC-ing. Examination of the historical and political contexts in which hip hop culture has taken shape. Attention to questions of race, gender, authenticity, consumption, commodification, globalization, and old-fashioned "funkiness." Includes three evening screenings.

courses.title: Innovations in U.S. Philanthropy
courses.description: Modern U.S. philanthropy has been institutionalized and evolving since Andrew Carnegie and John D. Rockefeller created perpetual foundations. This seminar interrogates the ethics of the enterprise’s power, how philanthropic strategies have evolved over the last century, and what that evolution means for democratic society. Those who practice philanthropy in the US are free to choose which problems to work on and their modes for doing so. The most well-known general-purpose foundations (such as Ford and MacArthur) are designed to be perpetual; others (including Gates) will spend down their resources; some have fostered politically conservative movements while others have championed progressive causes. Some funders act as social venture capitalists, creating new organizations or making mission-related investments; others practice trust-based philanthropy providing unrestricted funding to nonprofits. Some of today’s billionaires collaborate, others form for-profit LLCs, and others (like Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong) proclaim that "a lot of…philanthropies are actually net negative on the world." This seminar examines how private resources have been deployed for public purposes. Students analyze primary sources, debate major critiques and defenses, and develop an independent research project on a philanthropic strategy.

courses.title: Political Communications: Campaign Lab
courses.description: This seminar examines the inner workings, tactics, and strategies of modern political campaigns through the lens of strategic communications. Beyond engaging in analytical discussion and hearing from seasoned political operatives, students will participate in a series of four Campaign Labs, during  which they will demonstrate what they have learned in high stakes scenarios-—preparing a principal developing a message, prepping for debate, and running rapid response. By the end of this course, students should be able to:xplain the roles and responsibilities within each department on a modern political campaign; execute communications strategies and tactics (e.g., developing a message, pitching stories, prepping principals, writing speeches, running rapid response), and assess the strategic effectiveness of political campaigns in real time, with an eye toward the 2028 presidential election

courses.title: The Art of Travel Writing (Creative Writing)
courses.description: Travel writing is an act of sustained attention: to landscape, to movement, and above all to the people whose lives give a place its texture and meaning. At its best, first-person factual journey writing offers insight and testimony, and it is a genre that has adapted to be particularly reflective of the modern condition. Yet travel books have also contributed to imagined geographies that reinforce unequal relationships of power. Reading across global traditions of travel literature and contemporary reportage – from Ibn Battuta and Xu Xiake to Dervla Murphy, Amitav Ghosh, and Paul Salopek – we investigate how writers create authority on the page, and who gets to describe whom: the traveler and the travelee. Run as a writing workshop, the course begins with field notes and interview practice and moves toward carefully structured, substantially revised place-based essays. We pay particular attention to scene construction, character, point of view, voice, and detail. Travel here doesn’t mean distance: we are in New Haven, and the best subject may be something familiar and close to hand. Students finish the term with a portfolio of polished original work.

courses.title: Trials of the 20th Century
courses.description: An examination of several famous trials of the twentieth century, focusing on the legal significance, political and historical context and consequences, social implications, and media coverage of each case. Trials include the Lindbergh kidnapping case; the Scopes "Monkey Trial"; the Rosenberg spy case; the Chicago Seven conspiracy case; the O. J. Simpson and Emmett Till murder trials; the Scottsboro Boys case; the Rodney King case; the My Lai Massacre Court-Martial; and the impeachment trial of President Clinton.

courses.title: Art of the Printed Word
courses.description: Introduction to the art and historical development of letterpress printing. Examination of typographic design, the evolution of private presses, and contemporary printing practices. A historical survey of fine printing, complemented by a practical study of press operations using antique plate presses and the modern cylinder proof press. Topics include typesetting with both hand-set metal and digital type, paper stock and ink selection, basic hand-binding, computer-based design applications, and new technologies such as photopolymer plates. Materials fee: $100. Enrollment limited to 15.

courses.title: Exploring and Understanding White Collar Crime
courses.description: This course examines the many aspects of white collar crime; perjury, obstruction of justice, corporate crimes, Ponzi Schemes, insider trading, money laundering bribery and political corruption. The course explores how white collar crime, once virtually ignored by law enforcement has become a major focus of federal and state investigative agencies with massive resources allocated toward combatting it. The seminar examines the root causes of white collar crime as well as its pervasiveness in every day life.  Specific cases of white collar defendants, both individuals and corporations that have profoundly impacted business, law, science, healthcare and other disciplines are examined.

courses.description: Study of the basic virology and immunology of HIV/AIDS, along with its extraordinary historical and social effects. For students in all majors willing to engage primary scientific and medical research literature. Not open to students who have taken MCBD 065 or 0650.

courses.title: Journalism of Community and Connection
courses.description: This nonfiction writing seminar focuses on all facets of immersive, truthful storytelling. The broad theme of community that undergirds the readings, discussions, and assignments is open-ended and meant to encompass this particular place and time of life as well as the greater purpose of nonfiction storytelling. The skills this class nurtures are not limited to setting words on the page; various assignments and discussions cover the art of observing, interviewing, organizing ideas, and perhaps most importantly the ethics and morals spanning all journalistic work. The first two thirds of the semester contain a variety of short- and medium-length projects. The last part revolves around comprehensive longform pieces of substantial scope and depth undertaken in an area of keen individual interest. This ultimate goal of this class is to form its own community of writers who find within the group the comfort, support, and inspiration required to stretch themselves and their skills, to ask challenging questions about accountability and bias, and to seek underlying truth.

courses.title: The Psychology and Ethics of Persuasion
courses.description: Learning about the psychology of persuasion can help us to become more effective speakers and writers, but it should also lead us to ask important questions: How can we avoid being misled by the various forms of psychological influence to which we are all susceptible? Where should we draw the line between legitimate techniques of persuasion and unethical manipulation? What practical steps can we take to make our arguments about politics and other contentious topics more constructive and less acrimonious? This interdisciplinary course is intended to help you to develop a better understanding of the psychological and ethical complexities of persuasion, but its primary goal is practical: to help you develop skills and habits that will enable you to be an effective and ethical persuader while also learning to recognize and resist common tactics of manipulation.

courses.description: A graduate-level course, open to undergraduates, about elections, electoral politics, and electoral institutions in the United States. courses.title: Biology, the World, and Us
courses.description: This course is for non-science majors who wish to gain an understanding of modern biology by examining the scientific basis of current issues. We’ll consider issues related to:  i) pandemics and global infectious disease;  ii) the climate crisis;  iii) the future of genetics and the new green revolution. Many of the topics have an increasingly large impact on our daily lives.  The issues are both social and biological, and it’s crucial that social debate be based on a clear understanding of the underlying science.  The instructors will explain the scientific foundation beneath each issue.  We’ll emphasize the nature of science as a process of inquiry rather than a fixed body of terminology and facts.  The course is not intended to be a comprehensive survey of biology.

courses.description: Continuation of SCIE 020. This first-year seminar is the second of a two-part sequence designed for students in the Science, Technology and Research Scholars (STARS) program, and other first-year students interesting in studying the physical and mathematical sciences. In the second semester, students identify a Yale research mentor and prepare an independent grant proposal to prepare for summer research. The organizational structures and best practices associated with scientific research are examined. Credit for SCIE 020 is given only upon successful completion of SCIE 021.  One course credit, one SC or WR credit, is awarded after successful completion of both courses.

courses.title: Perspectives on Biological Research
courses.description:
The goal of this two course series is to introduce Science, Technology, and Research Scholars 1 (STARS1) passionate about conducting research in the life sciences to the outstanding research opportunities available to them. Thirteen Yale faculty, well known as excellent undergraduate research mentors, lecture on their own research and serve as potential future research mentors. Students emerge from this course with an appreciation for the diverse research conducted by Yale biologists. They also learn skills essential for any successful scientist, including how to (1) read the primary scientific literature on the research conducted by each faculty, (2) present this material to the class and, (3) write a grant proposal. Credit for SCIE 010 only on completion of SCIE 011; one course credit, one Sc credit or one WR credit, and guaranteed summer research funding is awarded for successful completion of the year's work. 

Prerequisite: SCIE 010. Students must take MCDB 201L concurrently with this class.

courses.title: Death in Sicily: Literature, Liturgy, Ritual, and Mortuary Politics
courses.description: From ancient journeys to the underworld to migrant deaths in the Mediterranean today, this course explores how people in Sicily have understood the passage between life and death. We bring poetry and philosophical reflection into conversation with funerary rituals, liturgy, tombs, sacred objects, and film, tracing how the island’s ancient cultures endure and change through centuries of migration and religious exchange. Christian burial rites, Jewish and Muslim practices, saints’ relics, and Palermo’s Capuchin Catacombs reveal how the dead remain part of everyday life, shaping religious devotion, artistic expression, and political struggles over land, borders, and memory. Combining literary analysis, historical inquiry, archaeology, liturgical studies, and ethnography with regular film screenings and close examination of material and visual evidence, the course invites students to explore death in Sicily through multiple methods and perspectives.

courses.title: Liturgical History
courses.description: This course surveys the history of Christian worship from its early Jewish and Mediterranean contexts through medieval Eastern and Western traditions, the Protestant and Catholic Reformations, and modern and global Christianity, including contemporary Protestant traditions. It explores how worship shapes Christian communities and how liturgical traditions acquire authority, sustain continuity, and undergo change. Close study of historical documents introduces the sources and methods of liturgical history, with particular attention to the relationship between prescribed rites and lived practice. Drawing on ritual and cultural studies, the course examines worship as embodied practice situated within particular social worlds, asking how it both reflects and shapes religious identities and relations of power. Lectures, discussion, student presentations, and three short papers develop the historical skills needed for further study of Christian worship.

courses.title: Hebrew Bible Textual Criticism and its Critics
courses.description: A practical and theoretical introduction to the textual criticism of the Hebrew Bible and other ancient Jewish texts. We gain familiarity with the tools scholars use to compare and evaluate variants and variance in these texts. We also engage with the history of textual criticism as a discipline and with recent debates over its nature and goals. How might scholars chart textual development without enshrining problematic assumptions about the "original" text? How does textual criticism work in situations of major variance, when the absence of a defined boundary between composition and transmission is especially clear? What are the implications of complex and nonlinear transmission histories for modern textual tools like editions and translations?
courses.classnotes: Prerequisites: one year or equivalent classical Hebrew, one year or equivalent ancient Greek.

courses.title: The Making of Christian Liturgy in Late Antiquity
courses.description: The late antique period (ca. third to seventh centuries CE) marks a crucial phase in the formation of Christian liturgy—one that may best be described as an era of "creative ritual experimentation." This course investigates the development of Christian liturgical discourse and practice (e.g., Baptism, Eucharist, occasional prayers) through the lens of three distinct yet interconnected categories of social actors central to the late antique religious world: church fathers, holy men, and ritual scribes. Drawing on textual (e.g., homilies, hagiography, hymnography), material (e.g., amulets, relics, ritual handbooks), and visual sources (e.g., frescoes, liturgical architecture) from across late antique Christendom—particularly Egypt, Syria, and Byzantium—students explore how liturgical traditions were articulated, performed, and contested in both ecclesiastical and everyday religious settings (e.g., households, saints’ shrines, local feasts). Prior coursework in liturgical studies, such as Foundations of Christian Worship, is helpful but not required.

courses.title: Writing Prayers
courses.description: In poetry, the lyric address refers to the "you" of a poem. Of course, in prayer, the "you" is most often either declared or assumed. How can we learn to write (and edit) prayers that serve purposes from private to public, using language in ways that is both pastoral as well as prophetic? Building on theopoetic analysis and readings of prayers and poetry, this class provides students with the capacity to write prayers in different registers, develop editorial skills, and both receive and give critical feedback. Some of the questions explored—in both readings and weekly assignments—are: what is the relationship of poetry to prayer? Does doctrine diminish the creativity of a poem? What role does form play in a prayer? Is community prayer a place for innovative theology, or should the emphasis be on communicating set ideas? How do concerns of justice, protest and assertion find place within a prayer? What does it mean to edit a prayer? This writing seminar is limited to twelve students. Roughly one third of the time is spent discussing assigned readings, with the rest of the time devoted to discussing contributions from the class. Admission to the class is on the basis of a paragraph detailing (1) interest in the class, (2) capacity to generate creative work, and (3) experience or willingness to respond fruitfully to critical engagement with the student’s contributions. Preference for second- and third-year students (but exceptions will be made for some first year students).
courses.classnotes: Preference for 2nd or 3rd year students, with consideration given to first year students with prior experience or capacity in writing.

courses.title: Bhakti and Bollywood
courses.description: The goal of this advanced language course is to develop students' overall language skills and cultural sensibility, and to provide additional knowledge of Early Hindi (Braj and Awadhi) language and literature, particularly medieval Bhakti (devotion) poetry of North India, through selected readings mostly written in Braj and Awadhi. Students begin with exploring "What is Bhakti" and "What is Bhakti and the Bhakti movement?" This is followed by the stories and biographies (hagiographies) of key poets followed by selected reading of the poetry of Surdas, Mira, Raskhan, Tulasidas and Kabir etc. that have been written in honor of Krishna, Ram and formless god of Nirgun Bhakti and has enjoyed great respect and influence on Indian cultural, art, music and society. The course explores the connection between Bhakti and Bollywood. Bhakti and Bhakti poets have influenced Bollywood in various ways. This connection is seen through Bollywood movies that portray the life and times of saint-poets and adopt their poetry directly. Sometimes this poetry is used on an occasion as a performance which has no direct connection with the main theme of the film, sometimes the same old content of poetry is echoed in modern Hindi songs, while some usages are very distant from their original form and context.
courses.requirements: Prerequisite: HNDI 1500 or instructor’s permission.

courses.title: Elementary Telugu II
courses.description: Through a variety of assessments, including script worksheets, oral pronunciation exercises, homework, and quizzes, students steadily improve their elementary language proficiency. The class uses audio-visual material rooted in everyday Telugu contexts to make the learning experience interactive and enable the students to acquire cultural knowledge while also being able to participate in conversations with confidence.

courses.title: Art and Ritual in Late Antiquity and Byzantium
courses.description: Christian ritual is fundamentally situational: it is a lived, multisensory experience that cannot be fully comprehended when divorced from the physical spaces and material objects that facilitated it, and much of what is important about it cannot be understood outside the specific context in which it occurs. This seminar explores the dynamic intersection of liturgy, art, and architecture in Early Christianity and the Byzantine Empire. By moving beyond purely text-based theological studies, we examine how sacred spaces, monumental images, and liturgical objects actively shaped—and were shaped by—the rituals performed within and around them. While the majority of the class is devoted to the Divine Liturgy, its architectural accommodation, and the art associated with it, we also investigate other rites, like baptism, marriage, and processions. The goal is not to create a neat narrative matching art and ritual but rather to consider both as products of specific historical, social, and theological circumstances.
courses.requirements: Prerequisite: a basic knowledge of Christian history.

courses.title: The Lives of Byzantine Saints
courses.description: Hagiography, the writing of a biography or life of a saint, is one of the most prevalent genres of Byzantine literature. Hundreds of Lives survive, ranging in date of composition from the fourth to the fifteenth centuries CE. They are written in various style and language registers by authors of differing capacities, some of whom were eyewitnesses, while others lived decades or even centuries after the saint had died. The protagonists of these Lives were all sorts and kinds, and included people from diverse backgrounds, professions, social classes, and experiences. The study of hagiography (sometimes called "critical hagiography") entails the scholarly engagement with such sources. While issues of authenticity and veracity dominated earlier scholarship, in recent years Byzantine Lives have been recognized as important sources for social, political, and religious history, for cult building, ideology, and propaganda, and windows to how Byzantines perceived and understood their world.
courses.requirements: Prerequisite: a basic knowledge of Christian history.

courses.title: Disturbance, Emergence, and Persistence: Urban Systems, Social Networks, and Disease
courses.description: Urban areas are simultaneously sites of ecological disturbance, engines of social and biophysical  emergence, and durable, path-dependent structures that persist long after the forces that created them have changed. This seminar with Yale School of Environment and Cary scientists asks how four bodies of theory—disturbance ecology, social-ecological systems, urban land system science, and disease ecology/zoonotic emergence—can be read together to understand cities and towns not as backdrops to disease and social dynamics, but as active ecological and evolutionary forces that generate novel pathogen-host-human configurations, reorganize social networks, and leave legacies that outlast the original disturbance events.

courses.title: Introduction to Sociology
courses.description: The class opens a doorway to sociology as an academic discipline. This is the systematic and rigorous study of society at all levels from the interpersonal, through institutions, organizations, and groups, to the level of the nation and world system. We cover the major research methods, forms of explanation, core concepts, and theoretical models. Substantive topics include inequality, race, gender, networks, culture, deviance, social change, and social behaviors among others.

courses.title: Environmental Security
courses.description: This graduate course examines the complex relationship between environmental change, natural resources, and national and global security. Drawing on frameworks from security studies, earth system science, political science, economics, international relations, and peace and conflict studies, students analyze how environmental stressors and resource competition—including climate change, biodiversity loss, water scarcity, land degradation, demand for critical minerals, energy and other natural resources—intersect with geopolitical instability, migration, and state fragility. The course emphasizes interdisciplinary approaches, combining quantitative environmental data with qualitative case studies from conflict zones, post-colonial contexts, and climate-vulnerable regions. Students engage with cutting-edge research, policy documents, and field-based accounts to develop analytical frameworks applicable to real-world security challenges. By the end of the course, students are equipped to assess environmental risk in security contexts, evaluate policy responses, and contribute to scholarly and practitioner debates at the nexus of ecology and conflict.

courses.title: Artificial Intelligence, Philosophically and Theologically Considered
courses.description: An investigation of ethical challenges posed by developments in artificial intelligence, with attention to how various philosophical positions and religious commitments might bear on these challenges. One significant focus is questions about whether machines could share in those features that give human beings their moral and spiritual significance. Could we build AIs that are capable of suffering or flourishing? Or that can appreciate beauty, exercise moral responsibility, or experience the divine? How should individuals and society navigate uncertainty and disagreement about the moral standing of AIs? Alongside these questions about the metaphysical and moral status of current and future AI systems, we will also consider how engagement with AI might affect human purpose and flourishing. Does intensive cognitive reliance on AI pose a threat to human autonomy and human excellence? How should we evaluate deployments of AI in religious contexts? What moral principles and values should guide AI behavior in a pluralistic society? Is the prospect of artificial "superintelligence" something we should welcome, or something that we should oppose?
courses.classnotes: This class is intended for Divinity students as well as doctoral students and sufficiently prepared college students.

courses.title: Music, Religion, and the Study of Korea
courses.description: This graduate seminar thinks with and beyond modern categories of music and religion in the study of twenty-first-century Korea. Recent articulations of disciplinary "turns" in music studies and religious studies—each toward the other—provoke a central question that grounds our course: What shifts in our understanding of Korean life occur when we refuse to relinquish the entanglement of religion and music in our interpretive praxis? Reading across ethnomusicology, religious studies, and anthropology, we first examine Korean religions—shamanism, Buddhism, Christianity—with one ear attentive to the undertow of music and sound. We then turn toward Korean music—especially jazz and K-pop—with the other ear attentive to the cantus firmus of religion. Finally, we zoom in and out of the center and fringes of Korean nationhood—gugak and unsounded musicalities—to contemplate how music and religion, reconstituted through their mutual entanglement, can shed light on contemporary Korean life in ways that propel forward our conversations in the humanistic study of the Pacific Basin.
courses.classnotes: Background in music studies, religious studies, and/or anthropology of Korea may be useful but is not expected or required.

courses.title: W.E.B. Du Bois and Black Radical Traditions
courses.description: This course examines W.E.B. Du Bois’s contributions to the study of religious, ethical, and political thought, especially on matters related to the enduring significance of chattel slavery and its afterlives, racialized capitalism and political economy, and black internationalist criticisms of American empire. The course also considers insurgent black activists and intellectuals whose contributions developed alongside and/or in response to Du Bois’s legacy. Those intellectuals include C.L.R. James, Claudia Jones, Martin Luther King, Jr., David Scott, Robert Gooding-Williams, Erica Edwards, Thulani Davis, and Jarvis Givens. The hope is to gain a richer appreciation of the expansiveness of black radical traditions in a way that deepens, expands, and resituates increasingly popular criticisms of race, patriarchy, economic inequality, and empire. Area V.
courses.classnotes: Students should have working familiarity with standard themes in African American studies and/or the intersection of religion, ethics, and politics more broadly.

courses.title: Ecological Ethics and Environmental Justice
courses.description: This seminar examines historical sources and recent debates within environmental and ecological ethics. It gives special attention to the influence of religious and theological worldviews; practices of ethical and spiritual formation; the land ethic; environmental movements for preservation and conservation; eco-feminism and womanism; and quests for economic, global, and environmental justice. The course draws from a range of intellectual and interdisciplinary approaches, including theology, philosophy, literature, sociology, anthropology, and postcolonial studies. Questions concerning race, place, empire, gender, and power are integral to our examination of these topics. Area V.

courses.title: Documentary, Fiction, Docufiction
courses.description: A seminar on the relationship between nonfictional and fictional media practice, with a particular focus on the "docufiction" form. Topics to be discussed include debates over the coherence of the notion of "documentary"; the epistemological and political claims of fiction and documentary; and the relationship of documentary and fictional practice to questions of nationhood, ethnicity, and gender. Films by directors such as Vertov, Eisenstein, Shub, Flaherty, Ivens, Visconti, Varda, Makavejev, Trinh Minh-ha, Costa, and Kiarostami.

courses.title: Critical Themes in Korean Popular Music
courses.description: This advanced seminar examines Korean popular music from academic perspectives informed by ethnomusicology, Korean studies, and transpacific studies. The course first historicizes the Korean music industry’s dialogical formation with modern political, economic, religious, and military forces such as Western imperialism, Protestant missions, Japanese colonization, the Cold War, military dictatorship, state-sponsored internationalization, and global technosociality. While the first half of the course emphasizes the Korean domestic industry, the second half pivots outward, focusing on reverse directional flows obtained in the late 20th and early 21st century. We interrogate K-pop’s role in constructions of Korea and Asia in the North Atlantic cultural imaginary and pay particular attention to continuities and disjunctures between K-pop and "world music," a genre conventionally marking non-Westerners’ colonial difference in the Western music industry. Themes such as race and racialization, gender and sexuality, migration and diaspora, voice and voicing, and media and technology inform our conversations throughout the semester.

courses.title: Psychoanalysis: Key Conceptual Differences between Freud and Lacan II
courses.description: This is the second part of a year-long seminar (first part CPLT 904) to introduce students to the discipline of psychoanalysis through primary sources, mainly from the Freudian and Lacanian corpuses. We rigorously study key concepts of continental psychoanalytic theory that students have heard or read about before but never had the chance to study. Students gain proficiency in what has been called "the language of psychoanalysis," as well as tools for their critical practice in humanities disciplines such as literary criticism, political theory, film studies, gender studies, theory of ideology, sociology, etc. Concepts studied include the unconscious, identification, the drive, repetition, the imaginary, the symbolic, the real, and jouissance. A central goal of the seminar is to disambiguate Freud's corpus from Lacan's return to it. We pay special attention to Freud's "three" (the ego, superego, and id) in comparison to Lacan's "three" (the imaginary, the symbolic, and the real). The corpus treated in this seminar comes from continental Europe and includes few materials from the Anglophone schools of psychoanalysis developed in England and the USA. During the second term and depending on the interests developed by the group in the first term, we devote five weeks to special psychoanalytic topics such as sexuation, perversion, fetishism, psychosis, anti-asylum movements, or to special circulations of psychoanalytic concepts across different disciplines, such as film theory or the critique of ideology. Commentators and critics of Freud and Lacan are also consulted (Michel Arrivé, Guy Le Gaufey, Jean Laplanche, André Green, Markos Zafiropoulos, and others). No previous knowledge of psychoanalysis is needed. We start at the beginning and the simplest questions are the most useful. Graduate students from all departments and schools on campus are welcome. Taught in English. Materials can be provided to cover the linguistic range of the group.
courses.requirements: Prerequisite: CPLT 904.

courses.title: Ekphrasis and Art Criticism
courses.description: Ekphrasis in its ancient Greek sense refers to the vivid description of an object, animal, person, place, scene, or event undertaken as an exercise in oral rhetoric. In that original context, the practice of ekphrasis was meant to "paint" a picture in the mind of the listener, and thus pointed to both the imagistic capacities of verbal language, and the integral link between the image and the imagination. In the twentieth century, ekphrasis acquired a narrower meaning: poetry addressed to or modeled on works of visual art. While informed by both of those understandings, this seminar considers ekphrasis both more broadly, in terms of genre, and more narrowly, in relation to a partial history of art criticism as a modern form of writing in the anglophone and European worlds, with a focus on the eighteenth through the twentieth century. It treats the different writerly modes now understood to be embraced by the term ekphrasis: not only poetry, but also the prose poem and the novel, as well as the Salon and art review. It also touches on such issues as the Renaissance inversion of the phrase ut pictura poesis; the competition between the arts of word and image; the presence or absence of illustrations; the modern relations between genres and mediums and the question of mediation; and the address of the different arts to the subjectivity of the reader/spectator. In addition to weekly presentations, a short preliminary paper, and a final research paper, students organize and contribute to a workshop on ekphrasis based on their own ekphrastic exercises, undertaken in the Yale Art Gallery. (Some class time is devoted to those exercises.) This seminar is the second of two (the first is HSAR 667); our hope is that students from both seminars will collaborate on this final event.

courses.title: Other Worlds in Science, Literature, and Philosophy
courses.description: It is odd, paradoxical even, that the so-called modern world should begin with a question, what is world, and should lead to a skeptical version of the question, are there other worlds? This course studies the strange phenomenon of thinking, writing, art-making, and dreaming of other worlds in European culture since about the 17th century. This is a trope or a dream that crosses disciplines, so we will read works from physical astronomy, philosophy, literature, and science fiction. Our hypothesis will be that the question of worlds was posed philosophically first by Leibniz, in his Protogaea (1719) and Monadology (1714), even though it had been roiling astronomy for a century or so. The class will have two philosophical touchstones, Leibniz and Heidegger, and two literary touchstones, Paul Scheerbart (Lesabendio) and Ursula K. LeGuin (The Left Hand of Darkness). With these works, and others, we hope to understand the drive to have a world (not merely a planet), even if it requires finding another.

courses.title: Infrastructures of Empire: Control and (In)security in the Global South
courses.description: This advanced seminar examines the role that infrastructure plays in producing uneven geographies of power historically and in the "colonial present" (Gregory 2006). After defining terms and exploring the ways that infrastructure has been conceptualized and studied, we analyze how different types of infrastructure (energy, roads, people, and so on) constitute the material and social world of empire. At the same time, infrastructure is not an uncontested arena: it often serves as a key site of political struggle or even enters the fray as an unruly actor itself, thus conditioning possibilities for anti-imperial and decolonial practice. The geographic focus of this course is the African continent, but we explore comparative cases in other regions of the majority and minority world.

courses.title: Gothic/Revival
courses.description: This graduate travel seminar focuses on the art and architecture of medieval England and its refraction and reconstruction through the Gothic revival of the late-eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. We study medieval monuments and sites, including Westminster Abbey and the Palace of Westminster, Canterbury Cathedral, Lincoln Cathedral, and York Minster, as well as collegiate architecture at Cambridge and secular structures including guildhalls and fortifications. Looking at architecture and sculpture in situ, we consider how nineteenth-century thinking has shaped the historiography of medieval art and how Victorian restoration and reconstruction transformed Gothic buildings. Contemporary scholarship is placed in conversation with texts by Horace Walpole, Thomas Carlyle, John Ruskin, and William Morris.

courses.title: The Senior Essay
courses.description: Independent research on the senior essay. By the end of the sixth week of classes, a rough draft of the entire essay should be completed. By the end of the last week of classes (fall term) or three weeks before the end of classes (spring term), two copies of the final essay must be submitted.

courses.title: Socio-ecology of water in Eastern Africa
courses.description: This seminar course provides students with an overview of topics critical to the understanding of the outcomes of human manipulation of surface and ground water. Students will examine how water, a natural product, is used as a source of socio-political power, how the locus of this power has shifted in the post-colonial nation state and the impacts on varied demographics. This course focuses on Eastern Africa, a region that borders the Indian Ocean and is climatically diverse. Comparative case studies also be included. Students explore the socio-ecology of water in societies living in contexts of climate change, population pressure, water pollution, and water commodification. They examine changing beliefs in water rights, the role of water in food security, and the importance of water towers in conservation. The course also offers students opportunities to critically appraise successful water projects and propose solutions to problems discussed in this seminar. At the end of the course, students are expected to broadly understand topics on the nexus of water and human action, and their social, political, and economic dimensions in a global south region.

courses.title: Topics in Human Sexuality
courses.description: In 1970, Yale professors and sexuality scholars Lorna and Philip Sarrel introduced what came to be their wildly popular lecture, "Topics in Human Sexuality." The course, offered at the height of the sexual revolution and shortly after Yale University admitted women undergraduates, was multipurpose: to teach students about pressing, contemporary social problems around sex, gender, and sexuality; to help students learn about their bodies, sexualities, and relationships; to direct students to resources and information about their sexual and reproductive health; and to advance the mission of a liberal arts education, namely, the cultivation of well-rounded, critically engaged, curious, participatory young citizens. This iteration of the course is inspired by the Sarrels’ ambitions, even if we are unlikely to realize them in full. The course is offered in the spirit of a critical sexuality education, critical as in 1) theory- rather than practicum-driven, but nonetheless 2) urgent. As political movements that endanger transgender children, suppress sexual expression, and rescind reproductive rights gain traction, the course offers candid, careful focus on: abortion, sexual education, queer and trans kids, pornography, university sexual politics, hooking up, and breaking up.  Along the way, we watch a season of Netlfix’s "Sex Education" together. The class (nonexclusively) focuses on social and political problems in the contemporary United States, and examines those problems by drawing upon scholarship in Gender & Sexuality Studies, American Studies, Sociology, Psychology, and Public Law.

courses.title: Gender, Sexuality, and U.S. Empire
courses.description: This course explores the cultural history of America’s relationship to the world across the long twentieth century with particular attention to the significance of gender, sexuality, and race. We locate U.S. culture and politics within an international dynamic, exposing the interrelatedness of domestic and foreign affairs. While exploring specific geopolitical events like the Spanish-American War, World War I and II, and the Cold War, this course emphasizes the political importance of culture and ideology rather than offering a formal overview of U.S. foreign policy. How have Americans across the twentieth century drawn from ideas about gender to understand their country’s relationship to the wider world? In what ways have gendered ideologies and gendered approaches to politics shaped America’s performance on the world’s stage? How have geopolitical events impacted the construction of race and gender on the home front? In the most general sense, this course is designed to encourage students to understand American cultural and gender history as the product of America’s engagement with the world. In so doing, we explore the rise of U.S. global power as an enterprise deeply related to conceptions of race, sexuality, and gender. We also examine films, political speeches, visual culture, music, and popular culture.

courses.title: Technocapitalism
courses.description: Technologies, especially digital tech and practices from nanotech to autonomous robots to big data and algorithmic finance have become a key issue in debates over shifts in capitalism, colonialism, militarism, and empire. Often imagined as placeless or as a "cloud," technocapitalism remakes geographies through its infrastructures and its practices of value generation. This course approaches techno-capitalism from an angle: It asks: how does technocapitalism make use of, and reproduce, difference? What is the significance of race, gender, class, and difference in shaping the techniques, practices, and logics of technocapitalism? Moving from a consideration of technocapitalism as a form of racial capitalism, this course uses scholarly text alongside film and fiction to explore the making of difference through built environments, planetary extraction, and the making of digital subjects.

courses.title: Environmental Politics
courses.description: Climate change, coupled with relentless pressure on the earth’s resources, has intensified the need for policy responses at local, national, and global levels. Yet breakdowns in political leadership, public disenchantment, and popular backlash mean that we must also consider what it means to build a meaningful environmental politics in the 21st century: What issues speak to most Americans, what arguments might prove effective, what changes are needed in existing institutions? We address these questions by looking at the history, evolution, and dynamics of environmental politics in the United States, with a focus on events since the 1960s. The course is designed with the following aims: learn about major stages in American environmental thought and their reflection in policy; gain an overview of key environmental writings, actors, institutions, processes, and events; explore important policy concepts (e.g., risk, regulation, sustainability, environmental justice); relate US environmental politics to developments in other countries and emerging global perspectives; and develop critical tools for environmental policy analysis. Through this work, students gain critical insight into what Americans historically valued about the environment and how agreement might again be forged on the purposes of environmental politics.

courses.title: Making Ancient Art
courses.description: Scholars have long recognized the crucial role of materials, techniques, and artisanal knowledge in the art and architecture of the ancient Mediterranean. We know, for instance, that developments in bronze casting were important for the rise of Greek naturalism, that chryselephantine techniques impacted religious iconography, and that added pigments transformed the visual effect of ancient statuary and architectural structures. Building upon such insights, in this seminar we seek to move beyond existing scholarship to consider how medium, facture, and makers’ agency may inform our understanding of various aspects of ancient art and architecture, such as the hierarchies among art forms and media, the relationship between art and text, or the status of artists and artisans in ancient societies. We read ancient accounts related to materials, art making, and craftsmanship, along with recent theoretical interventions in the disciplines of anthropology, archaeology, and art history. And we consider what ancient artifacts and material remains may tell us during hands-on sessions using the Yale collections. As part of the Yale-Cornell Consortium for the Study of Ancient Art, this course also brings students of both institutions together in a workshop to be held at the Museum of Fine Arts in Boston. Students develop research papers based on objects in the MFA collections and have a chance to learn about curatorial approaches and careers from museum experts.

courses.title: Word and Image in Medieval Art
courses.description: This seminar explores the communicative power of medieval European art by examining how images relate to textual content. By looking closely at images in manuscripts and other pictorial media in conjunction with affiliated writings, we see not only how visual forms could convey verbal subject matter but also how they might exceed, digress from, or even subvert it, opening up new channels for interpretation and imagination. Along with our classroom discussions, we engage with materials at the Beinecke Library, Yale Art Gallery, and the Met Cloisters.

courses.title: African Independence: A Cup of Plenty or a Poisoned Chalice?
courses.description: In every African colony after World War Two there emerged nationalist movements which no longer called for civil rights as in the pre-war years but demanded self-determination. While many of them got it easy, some had to fight long and bloody wars for it. By the 1960s the colonial edifice had crumbled except for the few settler colonies in southern Africa. But even here the winds of change could not be stopped. But what did decolonization and independence mean to Africa? Did Africans get what they wanted? Was independence a cup of plenty or a poisoned chalice? In addressing these questions, this course charts the economic, political, and cultural transformations of postcolonial Africa from the 1960s to the present. The argument is this: there can be no understanding of Africa’s challenges today without an inquiry into the nature of what the continent got from the departing colonial powers.

courses.title: The Making of Japan's Great Peace, 1550–1850
courses.description: Examination of how, after centuries of war in Japan and overseas, the Tokugawa shogunate built a peace that lasted more than 200 years. Japan's urban revolution, the eradication of Christianity, the Japanese discovery of Europe, and the question of whether Tokugawa Japan is a rare example of a complex and populous society that achieved ecological sustainability.
